notes.title: An Ode to Restraint: Lessons from the Tim Cook Legacy
notes.text: Market cap rose from $1.68 billion at the start of Jobs's tenure to over $4 trillion at end-2025; Cook added $3.64 trillion. Jobs-era price appreciation 47.19% a year compounded (1997-2011). Revenue grew 23.67% a year under Jobs and 8.52% (2012-2025) under Cook, with nearly $800 billion of buybacks, dividends since 2012 and a $17 billion debt issue in 2013; net debt always negative. Its share of Mag Seven capex fell from 8.04% to 3.02%. He calls it a mature, cash-returning, cautious business and says he has been a shareholder through much of both tenures.

notes.title: Trillion Dollar Market Caps: Fairy Tale Pricing or Business Marvels?
notes.text: Market cap went from $1 trillion to $3 trillion between 2018 and 2022, revenue up 72%, net profit almost doubled; revenue and net income about four times Nvidia's. Buying in 2018, 2020 or 2022 produced winning returns over one to two years. Breakeven revenue exceeds $1 trillion by year 5; already more than a third of the way.

notes.title: Just do it! Brand Name Lessons from Nike'sTroubles!
notes.text: A company where brand, operating system, design and app ecosystem combine, making brand value hard to isolate.

notes.title: The Corporate Life Cycle: Managing, Valuation and Investing Implications!
notes.text: Reincarnation case study (2000), a rare mature-company revival.

notes.title: The Seven Samurai: How Big Tech Rescued the Market in 2023!
notes.text: Value $176.79 vs price $188.00, about 6.34% overvalued (revenue CAGR 7.5%, target margin 36%, cost of capital 8.64%, IRR 7.89%). Within striking distance of value.

notes.title: Disagreements and First Principles: The Pushback on my Tesla Valuation
notes.text: The only firm on a list of large-revenue companies that earns double-digit margins apart from oil companies.

notes.title: Back to Earth or Temporary Setback? Revisiting the FANGAM Stocks
notes.text: Sep 2020 view: significantly overvalued, so he sold. Feb 2022: positioned itself as a privacy protector and hurt rivals such as Facebook; new iPhones well received. Does not own it now and will buy after a price dip.

notes.title: Illusion, Perception and Reality: Stock Splits and Index Inclusions
notes.text: The 4-for-1 split is cosmetic and does not change value (his hypothetical: $500 before, $125 after).

notes.title: A Viral Market Update XIII: The Strong (FANGAM) get stronger!
notes.text: Most overvalued of FANGAM, by more than 30% (IRR 5.30%). Sold on Aug 19, 2020 as the market cap crossed $2 trillion.

notes.title: A Viral Market Update XIII: The Strong (FANGAM) get stronger!
notes.text: Most overvalued FANGAM stock.

notes.title: Investing Whiplash: Looking for Closure with Apple and Amazon!
notes.text: Value about $200 in September, $197 in November (after updating the ERP to 5.68% and the 10-year at 3.01%); price $220 in September and $179 on Nov 30: from 9.54% overvalued to 9.14% undervalued. Sold short at a $230 limit (filled Oct 3), covered at $205 on Nov 5 for a profit, and bought at $175. Rule: buy at the 40th percentile of the value distribution and sell at the 60th.

notes.title: An October Surprise? Making Sense of the Market Mayhem!
notes.text: Short position opened at the start of October offset part of the market-wide losses.

notes.title: Amazon and Apple at a Trillion $: A Follow-up on Uncertainty and Catalysts!
notes.text: Value $200 (simulation 10th-90th percentile $176-229; revenue growth about 3%, margin falling from 30% to 25%, cost of capital 8.20%) vs a $219 price on Sept 18. Sold his shares at $220 on Sept 21 and placed a limit short order at $230, about the 90th percentile of value.

notes.title: Apple and Amazon at a Trillion $: Looking Back and Looking Forward!
notes.text: Value $200 vs price $219 (Sept 18, 2018): overvalued by about 9%. "Predominately a smart phone company" with about 62% of revenue from the iPhone, a maturing and competitive business; operating margin falls from 30% to about 25% over five years. 2014-2018: returned $277 billion ($61 billion dividends, $216 billion buybacks) vs $242 billion of free cash flow to equity. Leaned toward selling.

notes.title: Trillion Dollar Toppers: Market Triggers, Value Drivers and Pricing Catalysts!
notes.text: Triggers like a trillion-dollar market cap are unlikely to change value, though they may draw attention; he owns Apple shares.

notes.title: Apple: The Greatest Cash Machine in History?
notes.text: Held Apple 2010-2012, sold in April 2012, bought again in 2015 below his estimate and held through the rally. Earlier values: about $130 in Aug 2015 (price $110) and about $126 in Feb 2016 ($94). Slow revenue growth, margins declining with smartphone competition, possible larger tax bill on trapped cash. Sell trigger set at $140 a share, the top of his value range.

notes.title: Fairness Opinions: Fix them or Flush them!
notes.text: Illustrative valuation from his May 2016 analysis: values range from $80.81 to $415.63, and a $160 price sits at about the 92nd percentile: "possible, but neither plausible, nor probable." Used to argue for reforming fairness opinions.

notes.title: Icahn exits, Buffett enters, Whither Apple? Value and Price Effects of Big Name Investing
notes.text: Carl Icahn sold his entire stake (Apr 28, 2016); his 2015 letter argued $240 a share (2016 EPS $12 at P/E 18 plus $24.44 of cash per share), which Damodaran calls "casual pricing," not intrinsic value. Berkshire Hathaway (Combs and Weschler) took a new stake (May 16, 2016). He agrees Apple is a mature company whose cash flows can cover dividends. Prior post put the price at about $93.

notes.title: DCF Myth 3.2: If you don't look, its not there!
notes.text: Monte Carlo valuation: $126.47 base case vs about $93 (under a 10% probability the stock is worth less than $93). Revenue growth cut to 1.50% (from 2.2% in his Feb 2016 valuation of $129.80), margin centered on 25%, growth-margin correlation 0.50, cash of about $232 billion net of an expected $28 billion tax liability. Is again an Apple shareholder after selling in summer 2015.

notes.title: Race to the top: The Duel between Alphabet and Apple!
notes.text: Value $126 vs $94 price: undervalued by about 25%. Prefers Apple as an investment; sees Alphabet as the better business and momentum trade.

notes.title: A Violent Earnings Season: Pricing and Value Perspectives
notes.text: Used as a price-versus-value example in a post on earnings season; no new valuation.

notes.title: Narrative Resets: Revisiting a Tech Trio (Apple, Facebook and Twitter)
notes.text: Value about $130 a share vs a price under $110 (down from $128 in March). Mature company with revenue growth under 5%, margin pressure offset by strong iPhone 6 margins, a small chance of another disruptive product; Apple Pay a possible breakthrough. Waiting a few weeks before buying; expects to be a shareholder again.

notes.title: Reacting to Earnings Reports: Let's get real!
notes.text: Value $96.55/share; plans to exit if price reaches $100, otherwise holds.

notes.title: Watch the Gap: Apple's long and twisted pricing journey
notes.text: Value $648-675 a share (his table lists $674 on Apr 24; later $675 after a share-count correction to 861.38 million) vs $525 before earnings and $594 at the post: about 12% below value. Revenue growth about 5% with margin pressure; buybacks and dividends do not change operating asset value; the 7-for-1 split is cosmetic; a further $17 billion bond issue adds about $5 a share. "I will continue to hold Apple but I have learned to remain vigilant."

notes.title: The Brand Name Advantage: Valuable, Sustainable and Elusive
notes.text: Cites Interbrand's $98.3 billion brand value; says Apple's price premium is only partly brand (software, features and quality matter too).

notes.title: Rebirth and Reincarnation: Escaping the corporate death spiral
notes.text: Valued at $600 a share; a good investment but he does not yet see the ingredients for rebirth, so he waits.

notes.title: Apple: News, Noise and Value
notes.text: Value about $588 vs $420 on Apr 28, 2013, after lowering revenue growth and target margins and adding debt; the price already implies low growth and declining margins. Hold.

notes.title: Hundred dollar bills are hard to come by!
notes.text: Argues Apple's cash cannot be unlocked easily and criticizes Cook's communication with investors.

notes.title: Financial Alchemy: David Einhorn's "value" play for Apple
notes.text: Einhorn's preferred-stock proposal creates no value, though it might act as a price catalyst.

notes.title: Back to Apple: Thoughts on value, price and the confidence gap
notes.text: Value $608 vs $440 (about 90% chance undervalued); a large value-price gap may not close quickly because of the confidence gap. Holds it, capped at 10% of his portfolio.

notes.title: Market Mayhem: Lessons for Apple
notes.text: Advice to Apple after the market mayhem: rebuild investor trust, be more transparent, choose a growth or mature identity and act on it, pursue disruption in new markets.

notes.title: Are you a value investor? Take the Apple test
notes.text: Value $609 a share vs $440 (about 38% upside). Buy for value investors who pass the gut and confidence checks; he bought at $500 and does not plan to add.

notes.title: Apple's Crown Jewel: Valuing the iPhone Franchise
notes.text: Values the iPhone franchise at about $307 billion using a product life-cycle model (margins, two-year upgrade cycle, customer switching), roughly half of the $623.5 billion market value reached on Aug 20. No explicit call; he sold in April 2012.

notes.title: Earnings surprises, price reaction and value
notes.text: Earnings-surprise post: a pre-report valuation spreadsheet is linked; no value stated; readers judge how the report affects their strategy. He sold his shares in April 2012.

stocks.summary: Damodaran's most-covered stock, and the one he trades most. He valued it undervalued in 2013 and 2015-16 (about $126-130 vs prices in the $90s-$110s) and overvalued in 2018 ($200 vs $219) and again in 2020, selling each time the price ran ahead; by 2024 he had it about 6% overvalued ($176.79 vs $188). He treats it as a mature smartphone company where brand, ecosystem and services are hard to separate, argues a trillion-dollar market cap or stock split changes nothing about value, and in 2026 reviews Jobs vs Cook era value creation.

stocks.name: S&P 500 index

notes.title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
notes.text: Fell 4% on Nov 5, 2026; AI companies' share of US equity market cap peaked at about 37% on Sept 30, 2026. AI stocks lost almost $1.8 trillion of market cap on Nov 5 alone.

notes.title: The Anthropic Feedback Loop: The Cost of Capital Delusion and Diversion!
notes.text: Implied expected return 8.99% at the start of October 2026 with a forward PE near 20; he argues a cost of equity above 10% is hard to justify.

notes.title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
notes.text: Companies returned 63% of earnings to shareholders in the twelve months into 2026, a low not seen since 2004. Implied expected return rose from 8.41% to 8.99%; implied equity risk premium 3.70% (below 4% for the first time this year). Not a market timer, so no verdict.

notes.title: Interest Rates and Stock Prices: An Old Debate Flares up!
notes.text: Rose strongly in the first eight months of 2026. On days the 10-year yield rose more than 3 bp the index fell about half a percent on average, and rose about half a percent when it fell. Analysts' 2026-27 earnings estimates rose more than 11%, the main reason equities held up. Technology aggregate return 25.22% but the median tech company only 7.75%, so gains were concentrated in the largest firms. No valuation call.

notes.title: Country Risk: Drivers, Measures and Investment Implications - The 2026 Edition!
notes.text: At 7,499.36 on July 1, 2026; implied equity risk premium 4.42% (4.20% after a 0.22% default spread for the US Aa1 rating).

notes.title: SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic: The S&P 500 Inclusion Question and Investment Consequences!
notes.text: Closed at 7554.29 on June 15, 2026, float-adjusted market cap $63,498 billion; covers over 80% of US market cap. Inclusion effects have faded (S&P study of 715 additions, 1995-2021).

notes.title: Oil, War and the Global Economy: The Market's Narrative in March 2026
notes.text: Implied ERP rose from 4.37% (Feb 27) to 4.77% (Mar 31) after the Iran war began; he calls the rise modest and says the decline reflects inflation and growth concerns, not panic. VIX rose from 19.86 to 25.25, smaller than in March 2020 or April 2025.

notes.title: The Price of Risk: An Equity Risk Premium Monologue!
notes.text: Implied ERP 4.23% at the start of 2026, 4.37% at the start of March and 4.51% by March 13 (index fell Feb 27-Mar 13 while oil rose above $100). Stocks look richly priced on P/E and dividend yield but the implied ERP is "in line" with the 65-year US average. Not clearly over- or undervalued; the market seems too sanguine about catastrophic risk. Historical-premium methods would have given roughly 5.5% to 14.5%.

notes.title: Data Update 8 for 2026: Time for Harvesting - Dividends and Buybacks
notes.text: Dividend yield has declined since 1960: about half of expected returns came from dividends in 1960 vs under 15% in 2025. US buybacks totaled $1.153 trillion in 2025, about 60% of cash returned.

notes.title: Data Update 2 for 2026: Equities get tested, and pass again!
notes.text: Rose from 5881.6 to 6845.5 in 2025, a 16.39% price return (17.72% total), 45th of 98 years. Implied ERP 4.23%. At a 2% ERP he estimates 14,834 (53% undervalued); at 6%, 4,790 (43% overvalued). He is holding back on putting idle cash into US equities and prefers T-bills. Mag Seven share of US equity rose from 11% in 2014 to 30.89%.

notes.title: Data Update 1 for 2026: The Push and Pull of Data!
notes.text: US equity market (5,994 firms, $69.8 trillion) up about 16.8% in 2025; China up 32.5% in dollars, India up 3.31%. No valuation view.

notes.title: Trillion Dollar Market Caps: Fairy Tale Pricing or Business Marvels?
notes.text: Implied cost of equity about 8% at the start of November 2025.

notes.title: A Golden Year (2025): Gold's Price Surge - The Signal in the Noise!
notes.text: Implied equity risk premium 4.03% at the start of October 2025.

notes.title: A "Fairly Highly Valued" Market: A Fed Chair Opines on Stocks, but should we listen?
notes.text: Fell 14.3% to the April 8 bottom then rose 13.7% year to date through Q3. Agrees with Powell that stocks are "fairly highly valued": 15-year return about 18.74% a year vs 9.94% over the century, with elevated PE, CAPE and equity risk premium readings. Magnificent Seven are 30.35% of US market cap and 52.4% of the 2025 gain.

notes.title: A "Fairly Highly Valued" Market: A Fed Chair Opines on Stocks, but should we listen?
notes.text: Intrinsic value about 5,940, roughly 12.6% below its Sept 30, 2025 level (ERP 4.25%, risk-free 4.16%, implied return 8.41%). Backtests from 1871 to 2025 found no CAPE-based timing rule that added to returns, so he does not time the market.

notes.title: Sovereign Ratings, Default Risk and Markets: The Moody's Downgrade Aftermath!
notes.text: Expected return 8.64% on May 30, 2025. The Moody's downgrade lowers the riskfree rate from 4.41% to 4.01% and raises the ERP from 4.23% to 4.63%; effects too small for investors to notice.

notes.title: The Greed & Fear Tango: The Markets in April 2025!
notes.text: Fell about 10% in the first two days of April then recovered to within 1% of the start-of-month level; implied ERP 4.59% to 4.58% after rising above 5%. VIX peaked at 52.33 on April 8 and ended at 24.70. Mag Seven down $2.6T year to date; he holds six of the seven.

notes.title: Anatomy of a Market Crisis: Tariffs, Markets and the Economy!
notes.text: US equities lost $5.3 trillion in the week (down 9.24% from March 28). Implied ERP rose from 4.57% on April 2 to 5.08%. Compares with 2008 (equities fell 28% from Sept 12 to Dec 31, ERP near 8%) and 2020 (down 33%, ERP 7.75%).

notes.title: Investing Politics: Globalization Backlash and Government Disruption!
notes.text: Implied ERP rose from 4.35% at the start of March to 4.68% in two weeks (4.28% on Election Day). Values the index at 5262 (set in January) vs 5882 at the start of the year; still above his estimate after the drawdown through March 10, since recent events lowered his fair value.

notes.title: Data Update 3 for 2025: The times they are a'changin'!
notes.text: Mag Seven added $5.6 trillion in 2024, nearly all of the market's gain, and $15.8 trillion over 2014-2024 (about 40% of the increase). Technology added $4.63 trillion in 2024. He argues the small-cap premium is not returning; large caps beat small caps by about 4-4.5% a year over 20 years; low price-to-book stocks have trailed by 0.87% a year since about 1990.

notes.title: Data Update 2 for 2024: A Stock Comeback - Winning the Expectations Game!
notes.text: He judged the index overvalued by about 9.2% at the stated levels. Seven companies (Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Tesla) drove a large share of the 2023 market-cap increase.

notes.title: Market Resilience or Investors In Denial? A Mid-year Assessment for 2023!
notes.text: Up about 16% from the start of 2023; assumes analyst earnings for 2023-2025 and long-term growth of 3.88% after 2027; fairly valued; macro forecasting and timing are unreliable; do not chase recent winners.

notes.title: Data Update 2 for 2023: A Rocky Year for Equities!
notes.text: 2022 total return -18.01%. Using analyst estimates and a 5% ERP, close to fair value; scenarios range from 4,311 (low inflation, no recession) to 3,212 (high inflation, steep recession).

notes.title: Reaping the Whirlwind: A September 2022 Inflation Update!
notes.text: "Very mildly over valued" on Sept 23, 2022: 10-year Treasury 3.69%, ERP 6.05% (from 4.24% on Jan 1), implied return 9.75%, 2023 earnings estimate 243.46. Keeps existing holdings; no direction bets.

notes.title: In Search of a Steady State: Inflation, Interest Rates and Value
notes.text: Value about 4,181 vs a 4,147 close on May 5: roughly in line (steady-state 10-year rate about 3%, ERP near 5.24%).

notes.title: Russia in Ukraine: Let Loose the Dogs of War!
notes.text: Value 4,197 vs about 4,431 on March 16, 2022: about 5.6% overvalued (target T-bond rate raised to 3%). Does not time the market; prefers company-level selection, with caution on tech growth and Russian equities.

notes.title: Data Update 2 for 2022: US Stocks kept winning in 2021, but...
notes.text: Index 4,766 at end of 2021, 4,533 at the update; stocks look expensive. Assumes analyst estimates for two years, growth fading to the risk-free rate, starting payout 77.36%, risk-free 1.51% rising to 2.5%, ERP 5%, implied return about 5.75%. DIY valuation; no recommendation.

notes.title: Investor Taxes and Stock Prices: Threading the Needle!
notes.text: At 4,201.62 on May 7: 5.73% pre-personal-tax and 5.01% post-tax expected return; a higher capital gains rate for the wealthiest (30% of holdings) would lift the required return to 6.05% and cut value about 7.09%.

notes.title: Interest Rates, Earning Growth and Equity Value: Investment Implications
notes.text: Best case worth 3,919, just above current levels (T-bond rate falling to 1.00%); significantly overvalued if rates reach 3% or more with earnings growth lagging by 0.5%.

notes.title: Data Update 2 for 2021: The Price of Risk!
notes.text: About 12% overvalued (implied equity risk premium 4.72% on Jan 1, 2021, risk-free rate rising toward 2%, consensus 2021-22 earnings then economy-rate growth, 5% fair ERP): "certainly not bubble territory." Holds more cash than usual and bought partial downside protection with derivatives.

notes.title: US Equities: Resilient Force or Case Study in Denial?
notes.text: Implied equity risk premium 5.55%: stocks not unduly priced; market-neutral.

notes.title: Interest Rates and Stock Prices: It's Complicated!
notes.text: Scenarios: more of the same about 2,250; return of inflation about 2,133; growth engine about 3,031; melded about 2,610 (about 3.1% below the March 2 level).

notes.title: Testing Times: Market Turmoil and Investment Serenity
notes.text: At 2,581 on Feb 8, 2018: about 3.9% undervalued on 7.26% earnings growth; about 16% overvalued at 3.03% growth. Does not time the market; revaluing every holding.

notes.title: A Tale of Two Markets: Politics and Investing!
notes.text: At 2,411.8: 7.50% expected return, 5.29% premium over a 2.21% 10-year Treasury: richly priced vs history, not vs alternatives.

notes.title: A Tale of Two Markets: Politics and Investing!
notes.text: Implied US equity risk premium 5.29% (June 1, 2017); low volatility sits beside high policy uncertainty; no market-timing call.

notes.title: Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble: The Costs and Benefits of Market Timing
notes.text: Implied equity risk premium 4.99%; fairly valued; market timing rarely pays: stay invested.

notes.title: A Sweet Spot for US Equities: Opportunity and Dangers
notes.text: Value near 1800 using a 4.71% equity risk premium; the rise is justifiable but a new macro crisis or sudden rate spike is the risk. No market timing.

notes.title: Reversal in Risk Premiums (or premia): The 2010 story
notes.text: Implied US equity risk premium fell to 4.36% (expected to rise toward 5%); multiples rebounded toward pre-crisis levels.

notes.title: Is it time to make the move?
notes.text: Implied US equity risk premium hit 5%; lists criteria for bottom-fishing resilient, cash-rich companies.

notes.title: The key number for stocks: The Equity Risk Premium (ERP)
notes.text: Tracks the equity risk premium day by day during the week of Sept 15, 2008; it rose in panic and fell in recovery.

stocks.summary: The market-level posts, mostly his monthly and annual updates. He computes the implied equity risk premium (about 4.0-4.6% through 2025-26, 4.42% in July 2026) and a fair-value index level, which has run from mildly overvalued to about 12% overvalued, and repeats that he does not time the market and that backtests of CAPE-based timing rules add nothing. Recent themes: Mag Seven concentration, buybacks ($1.153 trillion in 2025), the April 2025 tariff drop, the March 2026 Iran-war rise in risk premium, and the Nov 5, 2026 AI selloff that cut about $1.8 trillion in a day.

notes.title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
notes.text: Cited for dual-class shares that he holds. At its June 2012 IPO he judged Facebook overvalued at $36 a share, then bought at $18 about three months later.

notes.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
notes.text: Its Muse model is "obscured by Meta's advertising business."

notes.title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
notes.text: Hyperscaler with heavy AI capex, which will depress earnings and free cash flow until it pays off. He holds it.

notes.title: AI's Bar Mitzvah Moment: From Hype & Hope to Business Questions!
notes.text: One of the six hyperscalers in the capex chart; suggests testing whether its AI capex creates or destroys value with a breakeven spreadsheet.

notes.title: SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic: The S&P 500 Inclusion Question and Investment Consequences!
notes.text: Its Class B voting shares held by Zuckerberg are not counted in the index float, so it "punches in below its true weight."

notes.title: Revisiting the SpaceX Valuation: A Post-Prospectus Update!
notes.text: Traded at half its IPO price a few months after listing, to illustrate how IPO pricing can reverse.

notes.title: An Ode to Restraint: Lessons from the Tim Cook Legacy
notes.text: Praised for ad-ecosystem acquisitions (Instagram, WhatsApp) but criticized for the "expensive failed bet" on the Metaverse. Zuckerberg controls 57% of the votes with about 13% ownership; investors worry his AI bet could play out similarly.

notes.title: AI Scenarios: From Doomsday Destruction to Do-Nothing Bots!
notes.text: Cited with Amazon for negative market reactions to new AI investments.

notes.title: Data Update 7 for 2026: Debt and Taxes
notes.text: Its Louisiana data center joint venture with Blue Owl Capital may be a below-market loan or one with terms "no prudent lender would accept"; he calls this an unsustainable lending strategy.

notes.text: Market cap bumped by Llama; he criticizes its metaverse investment and the governance concerns it raises.

notes.title: META Lesson 3: Tell me a story!
notes.text: Feb 2022 valuation $346 a share vs $220 then; price just over $100 at the post. "Doomsday" scenario (advertising income frozen at trailing level, 20-year life, no liquidation value, R&D about $32 billion a year, Metaverse losses of $10 billion a year with no payoff, cost of capital 9%) gives equity value $258.6 billion, or $330 billion excluding the Metaverse, so Metaverse spending costs about $71 billion. Market cap $247 billion on Oct 29 and $311 billion on Nov 15 (implied Metaverse value destruction about $18.9 billion). Bought at $133 after the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and kept it; doubled his holding on Nov 4, 2022, an exception to his rule against doubling down. Admits he has no influence on management. Peers used: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Palantir, Snowflake, Uber, Airbnb, Twitter; FTX cited as a story-driven failure.

notes.title: META Lesson 2: Accounting Inconsistencies and Consequences
notes.text: Lesson 2 (accounting): reported profits understate earning power because R&D and Metaverse spending are expensed; trades at about 8x reported earnings, about 6x after adjusting for R&D and Reality Labs. Capitalizing R&D over 3 years gives adjusted net income of about $42.5 billion vs $28.8 billion reported.

notes.title: META Lesson 1: Corporate Governance
notes.text: Lesson 1 (corporate governance): argues governance should focus on shareholders' power to change management, not board composition or governance scores; reviews falling profitability and risks to the ad business.

Cut 2022 revenue by about 10%, margin from 35% to 32%, sales-to-capital from 1.50 to 1.20. "Not quite at the threshold of being a buy yet, but it is getting close": limit buy at $18; rejected selling puts at that level.

notes.title: Facebook: Sowing the wind, reaping the whirlwind
notes.text: IPO priced on momentum, not valuation: earlier estimate showed about a third overvalued; fell to about $32 after the IPO. Value investors should be ready to buy later; no immediate buy of Facebook or peers.

notes.title: Facebook and "Field of Dreams": Hoodies, Hubris and Hoopla
notes.text: Updated assumptions (growth about 45% compounded to $56 billion, 30% margin, $1.25 of revenue per reinvested dollar) still give $70-80 billion of equity, about $29 a share. "Long term sell": "far more downside than upside"; looking for the cheapest way to short it.

notes.title: Facebook and "Field of Dreams": Hoodies, Hubris and Hoopla
notes.text: Expects a modest 10-15% IPO pop that fades quickly; the best odds are a long-term short.

notes.title: The IPO of the decade? My valuation of Facebook
notes.text: Pre-IPO Facebook: base-case equity value about $71.6 billion (about $29.05 a share; Class A about $28), simulation median about $70 billion, 10% chance above $117 billion and 10% at or below $43 billion, vs a preliminary IPO range of $75-100 billion. Assumes 40% compound revenue growth for five years fading to the 2.01% risk-free rate by year 10, pre-tax margin from above 45% down to 35%, $1.50 of revenue per $1 of new capital, cost of capital 11.42% falling to 8%. Would not buy at $75 billion: the price assumes near-superlative success and the dual-class structure gives holders no say. "Could it be worth $100 billion? Sure, but you are fighting the odds as an investor."

stocks.summary: He valued pre-IPO Facebook at about $29 a share and called the $38 IPO a 'long-term sell', then bought at $18 after it fell. Later valuations: overvalued in 2013 ($27.65 vs $38), about fair in 2016, $181 vs $155 in 2018 (undervalued), the most undervalued FANGAM stock in 2020-22, and about fairly valued in 2024 ($445 vs $456). In 2022 he used Meta as a lessons series on governance, accounting for R&D and the metaverse; in 2025-26 he criticizes its metaverse spend, Blue Owl data-center financing and Zuckerberg's voting control, but says he holds it.

notes.title: Tesla in November 2023 : Story twists and turns, with value consequences!
notes.text: Value about $180 a share from a business-by-business breakdown (auto, energy, software, robotaxi); his January 2023 median was $153. Price below $200 (he cites $197): overvalued "at least based on my story." Trailing revenue $95.9 billion, operating income $10.7 billion (11.18% margin); auto gross margin 17.42% in Q3; energy 6.2% of revenue; Model 3 cut by $1,250 to about $39,000; FSD priced at $12,000 and still in beta; Cybertruck reservations over two million but he expects sales to fall short. History: bought at $180 in 2019 (market cap $32 billion) and sold too early at $150 billion in 2020; no Tesla in his portfolio in 2023; has a limit buy at $180 that may never fill.

notes.title: Disagreements and First Principles: The Pushback on my Tesla Valuation
notes.text: Value about $130 a share, "overvalued, albeit only mildly." Assumes revenue growth of 24% for five years (down from 35% in his Nov 2021 valuation), fading to 3.47% by 2032, revenue about $412 billion in 2032 with a growth wall near $400 billion; operating margin about 16% (17.93% in 2022); cost of capital 10.15% falling to 9%. $97 (December 2022) is a price at which he sees a good investment. Bought in 2019 and sold after about seven months. Skeptical of its autonomous-driving business because ride-sharing companies have struggled to make money.

notes.title: Tesla in 2023: A Return to Reality, The Start of the End or Time to Buy?
notes.text: Value about $130 a share (simulation median $120) vs $143 on Jan 25, 2023: overvalued. Assumes $400 billion of steady-state revenue, a 16% target operating margin, cost of capital 10.15%. No buy at current prices; buyers at $109 on 12/27/22 got a reasonable bargain. Discusses founder dependence and politics in investing.

notes.title: Tesla's Trillion Dollar Moment: A Valuation Revisit!
notes.text: Value per share $571 in his most upbeat scenario, less than half the market price: overvalued, and he would not invest; sold his shares in January 2020 and does not short because "momentum beats fundamentals" in the short term. Assumes revenue about $414 billion by 2032 (roughly ten million cars plus ancillary), a 16% operating margin, sales-to-capital 4.00, cost of capital 6% (risk-free 1.56%, ERP 4.62%), no failure risk; equity value about $692 billion ($640 billion for common). He admits he has repeatedly underestimated Tesla's value and calls it a "trade," not an "investment." Market cap rose from $2.8 billion (Aug 2010) to over $1 trillion.

notes.title: Illusion, Perception and Reality: Stock Splits and Index Inclusions
notes.text: Stock split and possible S&P 500 inclusion: no change in value, and inclusion unlikely to be a game changer.

notes.title: A Viral Market Update XIII: The Strong (FANGAM) get stronger!
notes.text: Sold his Tesla holdings in January 2020 at $640 (a split-adjusted price); the stock traded close to $2,000 at the post, which he flags.

notes.title: Tesla's Travails: Curfew for a Corporate Teenager?
notes.text: Value about $190 (simulation median $180; 10th percentile $52, 90th $380), after a price fall of almost 50% from about $360 in June 2018: close to fairly valued, slightly undervalued. Assumes $100 billion of revenue in 2028 and 10% pre-tax margins by 2023; failure risk raised from 5% to 20%; debt close to $14 billion. A "corporate teenager" with high potential. Bought: limit buy at $180, which executed. Shorting Uber and Lyft would pay more than buying Tesla, because autonomous cars will not roll out smoothly or soon. Calls the SolarCity acquisition an "unforced error."

notes.title: Tesla's Travails: Curfew for a Corporate Teenager?
notes.text: Adds: an acquisition floor at a $15 billion equity value (about $60 a share) adds roughly $10 a share to the simulated value; calls ARK Invest's model a forward pricing, not a valuation: its bear case adjusts to about $250 a share vs $560 on ARK's spreadsheet; the bull case is "closer to fiction." Expects the stock to test his patience.

notes.title: The Privatization of Tesla: Stray Tweet or Game Changing News
notes.text: Musk's tweet about going private at $420: Tesla does not fit the profile of a good buyout candidate; "secured funding" is questionable; a take-private would need roughly $55-60 billion; the episode may be tied to Musk's conflict with short sellers. His earlier value was about half the prevailing price. No trade.

notes.title: Share Count Confusion: Dilution, Employee Options and Multiple Share Classes!
notes.text: Share-count worked example: DCF value $189.23 a share (dilution captured in cash flows) or $171.99 after subtracting the value of outstanding options (169.76 million shares, 10.88 million options at a $105.56 weighted strike, worth $2,927 million); 88.06% of future capital needs funded with equity, 5% failure chance; an alternative case with a $200 issue price and 9% annual appreciation. Methodological; no trade.

notes.title: Twists and Turns in the Tesla Story : A Boring, Boneheaded Update!
notes.text: Revalued at about $186 a share vs a price of about $340; his optimistic "Royal Flush" scenario gives about $412. Story: revenue up tenfold to about $120 billion, pre-tax margin 12%, sales-to-capital about 2.25, cost of capital 8.29%, $14 billion of new capital in the royal flush case ($22 billion in his base case, with cash flows negative for eight years); production of about 30,000 cars a week by year 10. Debt is a survival risk for the next year or two. No explicit trade call, but "if you are bullish, that should scare you." Calls the 2016 SolarCity deal "ill-advised"; BMW (9.89% margin) is the benchmark.

Assumes about $93 billion of revenue in ten years (about 2 million cars), a 12% operating margin vs 6.33% for global autos, negative free cash flow for seven years and about $15.5 billion of new capital. Says the $1.5 billion junk bond offering makes no sense; he would issue equity (3-4% dilution) or low-coupon convertibles. Production is the harder challenge.

notes.title: Keystone Kop Valuations: Lazard, Evercore and the TSLA/SCTY Deal

notes.title: Tesla: It's a story stock, but what's the story?
notes.text: Valuation history: Sept 2013 $70 a share vs $168.76; July 2015 $123 vs $220; latest $151 (equity $25.8 billion, with the market cap at $33 billion), assuming a shift to a mass-market maker after almost 400,000 Model 3 deposits. "I will choose to sit this investment out." Says the SolarCity deal "muddies up the waters" (lower margins, more debt).

notes.title: Return to the firing line: Revisiting Tesla and hopefully living to tell the tale!
notes.text: Value $110-115 a share (range $99.85-118.47 depending on option treatment) vs a price of about $220: roughly half. Year-10 revenue $79.2 billion (cars plus batteries), a 12% margin, sales-to-capital 1.55, cost of capital 8.86% (from 10.03%), failure risk 0% (from 10%). Does not buy: expects to own it "sooner rather than later," but "Just not yet!"

notes.title: Return to the firing line: Revisiting Tesla and hopefully living to tell the tale!
notes.text: Updated upward from $67 to roughly $100-118 a share on revenue growth and a lower cost of capital; still overvalued (see main entry).

notes.title: Valuation of the week 1: A Tesla Test
notes.text: First "valuation of the week": $67.12 a share vs a $168.76 price; the simulation puts the odds of value exceeding price below 10%. Assumes revenue of about $64 billion (Audi-sized, roughly 60 times the trailing $1.33 billion), a 12.5% pre-tax margin, sales-to-capital 1.41, cost of capital 10.03% (60% auto, 40% technology), ERP 5.8%, a 10% failure chance (50% recovery), about $1 billion of NOLs. "I cannot see a rationale for buying the company at today's market price."

stocks.summary: Overvalued for most of a decade: $67 vs $169 (2013), $110-115 vs $220 (2014), $192 vs $365 (2017), $186 vs $340 (2018), $130 vs $143 (2023), then about fair at $183.75 vs $185 in Feb 2024 and about $150 in March 2025. He bought in 2019 near fair value, sold in January 2020 at $640, and exited fully by May 2025 after selling in the tariff selloff. He never shorted, citing momentum, argues Musk is a net positive to value, and in Dec 2025 shows Tesla needs 86% five-year revenue growth to justify its market cap.

notes.title: Apple and Amazon at a Trillion $: Looking Back and Looking Forward!
notes.text: Value $1,255 vs price $1,944: overvalued by almost 35%. A "Disruptive Platform" he admits he has consistently underestimated. Assumes 15% revenue growth to about $626 billion in 2027 and operating margin rising to 12.5% (about $78 billion). Implied joining the short sellers.

notes.title: Amazon: Glimpses of Shoeless Joe?
notes.text: Value $1,019 a share vs $1,460 on April 25, 2018. Three parts: retail/media (15% growth for five years, margin 9.09% to 12%), AWS (25% growth, margin falling to 20%), and Prime (100 million members, shipping costs growing slower than membership). A later Prime fee increase to $119 a year added about $100 a share to Prime's value. Not buying: has not owned it since 2012 and has a limit price at which he would return.

notes.title: Testing Times: Market Turmoil and Investment Serenity
notes.text: Revisiting after the February 2018 correction in case it brings the price within reach.

notes.title: Deconstructing Amazon Prime: Loss Leader or Value Creator?
notes.text: Values Amazon Prime separately: about $61-62 billion for existing members (96% renewal, $600 of incremental revenue per member growing 10% a year, operating margin 12.11% rising to 13%, shipping costs up 3% a year, cost of capital 8%), new members (15% growth for five years, $100 acquisition cost) and a corporate drag for about $1.6 billion of media costs. Prime is a valuable franchise; shipping costs are the key risk. The roughly $14 billion Whole Foods deal is a related move. No trade; he is a Prime member.

notes.title: The Disruptive Duo: Amazon and Netflix!
notes.text: Value $323.55 vs $507 price: overvalued. Neither bought nor shorted. Discusses GAAP treatment of its spending.

notes.title: "If you build it (revenues), they (profits) will come": Amazon's Field of Dreams!
notes.text: Base case ~$175 vs $295 price (overvalued); bullish case ~$345 needs a 12.84% operating margin. 'Not a winning game' at this price.

stocks.summary: Overvalued in every valuation from 2014 ($175 vs $295) to 2018 ($1,255 vs $1,944), which he admits he consistently underestimated; he took a short position in Oct 2018 as a market hedge. He valued Prime separately ($61-62 billion for existing members in 2017), bought again in 2022, found it about 8.6% overvalued in Feb 2024 ($155.72 vs $169.15), and holds it in 2026, citing Bezos's 'Field of Dreams' approach of scale before profit and treating it as a hyperscaler in the AI capex discussion.

notes.title: How much are you paying for growth?

notes.title: Growth and Value: Thoughts on Google, Groupon and Green Mountain

He argues a DOJ-style breakup makes little economic sense, notes Gemini and a 100-year bond, criticizes the Brin-Page voting control, and says in Oct 2026 that he holds it.

notes.title: The Scaling and Profitability Trade off: Venture Capital's Weakest Link!
notes.text: From his 2019 work: describing Uber as logistics rather than a car service could roughly triple its market. Also an example of low capital intensity in early scaling.

notes.title: AI's Bar Mitzvah Moment: From Hype & Hope to Business Questions!
notes.text: Cited with Airbnb and DoorDash as a smartphone-enabled intermediary that changed its industry.

notes.title: Revisiting the SpaceX Valuation: A Post-Prospectus Update!
notes.text: Cites its 2019 prospectus market size of $5.7 trillion as inflated; it lost more than 50% of its market cap in the year after its IPO, moving from overvalued to undervalued.

notes.title: A DIY (Do-It-Yourself) Valuation of Zomato
notes.text: Bill Gurley's critique of his narrow market definition changed his Uber valuation.

notes.title: The Market is Huge! Revisiting the Big Market Delusion
notes.text: Cited as a big-market-delusion example of price running ahead of value.

notes.title: IPO Lessons for Public Market Investors
notes.text: Value $35.42 vs $29.28 (about 17% undervalued), assuming drivers are employees under California law and global growth ambitions. Bought at about $30.

notes.title: Insights on VC Pricing: Lessons from Uber, WeWork and Peloton!
notes.text: Last VC round about $66 billion. Argues VCs set prices rather than value companies; calls the claimed $5.71 trillion addressable market overreaching. No purchase.

notes.title: Uber's Coming out Party: Personal Mobility Pioneer or Car Service on Steroids?
notes.text: Pre-IPO: about $54 a share top-down and about $51 rider-based, later updated to roughly $31-33 and $30 on a 1.8-2 billion share count. Top-down: $44.4 billion operating assets, $55.3 billion with stakes, about $61.7 billion equity; rider-based about $58.6 billion; pricing approach $47-124 billion. Rumored value $100 billion with about $10 billion raised. "Poised on a knife's edge": a personal-mobility business still unprofitable (prospectus: "may not achieve profitability"), valuation could exceed $100 billion if usage rises significantly. 91 million monthly riders, 5.2 billion rides; Uber Eats grew from 2.68% to 13.12% of net revenue; holds 20% of Didi, 23.2% of Grab and 38% of Yandex Taxi.

notes.title: User/Subscriber Economics: Value Dynamics
notes.text: User-based valuation follow-up: base value about $410 per user (simulated median about $414) vs about $900 per user implied by the reported $69 billion valuation, at the upper end of his simulated range ($74 to over $1,000). Expenses of about $9.3 billion split 48.17% servicing existing users, 41.08% acquiring users, 10.75% corporate. No trade: an exercise in process.

notes.title: User/Subscriber Economics: An Alternative View of Uber's Value
notes.text: User-based model: equity value about $37.2 billion vs the last private round of about $69 billion (about 46% below). Assumes a 15-year user lifetime, 95% annual renewal, 12% growth in revenue per user, 10% cost of capital for existing and 12% for new users, 25% user growth for five years, about $240 to acquire each new user. No trade.

notes.title: User/Subscriber Economics: An Alternative View of Uber's Value
notes.text: User-based model gives about $37.2B equity vs the ~$69B private round (about 46% below).

notes.title: Uber's bad week: Doomsday Scenario or Business Reset?
notes.text: Operating assets about $25 billion plus close to $11 billion of cash and its Didi stake, about $36 billion in total, vs a recent private round near $70 billion. A story shift, not a story break; 5% failure risk; treating drivers as employees would lower target margins; the story depends on the new CEO and the next round's pricing. Waits to revise until a CEO is named; no trade.

notes.title: Uber's bad week: Doomsday Scenario or Business Reset?
notes.text: Bad week is a story shift, not a story break: about $36B ($25B operating assets plus about $11B cash and Didi stake) vs about $69B, roughly 48% below.

notes.title: Dream Big or Stay Focused? Lyft's Counter to Uber!
notes.text: Value $23.4 billion vs an implied price of $51 billion. Conclusion: "At these prices, as I see it, Lyft is a better investment than Uber."

notes.title: On the Uber Rollercoaster: Narrative Tweaks, Twists and Turns!
notes.text: Revised value $23.4 billion (up from just under $6 billion in June 2014) vs about $51 billion in venture pricing; he says he was wrong in 2014 because his view of the market changed, not because of the VC price. Larger market (suburbs, shared rides, Asia; leaked 2015 gross billings $10.84 billion), fewer players with larger regional network benefits, an 80/20 driver split under pressure from Lyft, rising costs (driver classification, insurance, lobbying), contribution margins of 3.5% to 11.1% by city, low capital intensity for now. Invites readers to submit their own values.

notes.title: Up, up and away! A crowd-valuation of Uber!
notes.text: Private, so no price. A "crowd valuation": readers choose the narrative (market size, growth, share, revenue slice, reinvestment, risk). Range of firm values $799 million to $90.5 billion; uses a 12% cost of capital and sales-to-capital 5.00; 2014 gross receipts about $3.5 billion, with a 20% slice giving about $700 million of revenue. His own June 2014 estimate was $6 billion vs venture estimates of $17-18 billion and rumored values of $40 billion and up.

notes.title: Numbers and Narrative: Modeling, Story Telling and Investing
notes.text: Four narratives give values from $3.2 billion to $29.1 billion (plus a $2-3 billion disruption option); no market price. Used to illustrate tying numbers to a story.

notes.title: A Disruptive Cab Ride to Riches: The Uber Payoff
notes.text: Pre-IPO ($17 billion investor valuation): intrinsic operating-asset value about $5.9 billion. Assumes a $100 billion global taxi/limo market growing 6% a year to about $183 billion by 2024, 10% market share, Uber keeping 20% of gross receipts, a 40% steady-state margin, sales-to-capital 5.0, cost of capital falling from 12% to 8%, 10% failure probability. Overpriced; the median public-comparable multiple would give about $2.8 billion and venture-backed comparables just under $10 billion. Says Google and Tesla will leave Uber only "crumbs" in driverless cars.

stocks.summary: Pre-IPO he valued it at about $5.9 billion in 2014 vs a $17 billion investor valuation, then raised it to $23.4 billion in 2015 (admitting his view of the market changed), said Lyft was the better investment, and found it overvalued vs the $69 billion round in 2017 and the IPO in 2019. He bought at about $30 in Oct 2019 (value $35.42) as the price fell. He credits Bill Gurley's critique with changing his market definition and later cites its $5.7 trillion 'total market' as inflated.

Breakeven revenue about $483 billion (no growth wait) or about $678 billion if growth takes five years and equity receives a 2% cash yield; 8% cost of equity, 53.01% net margin, 64.44% ROE. Possible and plausible but hard to meet on probability as competition rises. No recommendation.

The most overvalued of the seven. He had sold half his holdings at $450 and planned to sell half of the remainder at $680.

notes.title: AI's Winners, Losers and Wannabes: An NVIDIA Valuation, with the AI Boost!
notes.text: Values it at about $240 a share as of June 10, 2023 when it traded at $409 (it rose to $434 by June 20): overvalued. Base case: revenue $267 billion in 2033 with AI chip revenue growing about tenfold, a 15% share of auto chips and 15% annual growth in gaming and other; R&D-adjusted operating margin 35% next year rising to 40% by 2027 (range 30-50%); sales-to-capital 1.15 vs 0.65 historically; cost of capital starting at 12.21% and drifting to 8.85%. A value above $400 is possible but unlikely; the price is "pushing towards the 95th percentile" and breakeven needs extraordinary growth plus margins near 50%. Bought in 2018 after a drop of over 50% and sold half at these prices, keeping the rest for optionality. Flags dependence on TSMC and China-Taiwan risk.

stocks.summary: He bought in 2018 as undervalued and saw it become a twenty-bagger after ChatGPT. His valuations were well below the price: about $240 vs $409 (June 2023), $436 vs $680 (Feb 2024, the most overvalued in his group), $87 vs $109 (Sept 2024), and $78 in Jan 2025. He sold most in April 2025, cut to a quarter by May, and sold the rest in four installments with no regrets; in Dec 2025 he frames the $5 trillion market cap by breakeven revenue (about $483-678 billion).

Assumes $11.5 billion of 2023 revenue (about 55% growth for five years), 25% pre-tax margin, $1.50 of revenue per $1 of capital, cost of capital 11.22% (beta 1.40), no taxes until year 5, about $1 billion of IPO cash. notes.title: Revisiting the SpaceX Valuation: A Post-Prospectus Update!
notes.text: Values enterprise value at $1.22 trillion and equity at $1.3 trillion, about $100 a share (the equity rises mostly from $75 billion of IPO cash). 2025 revenue grew about one-third (connectivity almost 50%, AI about 22%, space 7.64%); 2025 operating loss $2.57 billion, net loss about $5 billion. Raised AI target revenue from $80 billion to $160 billion but cut its target margin from 45% to 25%; space target margin 45%; connectivity 60%. Cost of capital 8.37% at the start and 8.25% in steady state. Book equity $41.3 billion, debt including leases $22.9 billion, cash $24.7 billion, 12,535 million shares. Calls the reported $28 trillion total addressable market "fantasy." An offering price near $135 a share (about $1.8 trillion) is "too richly priced" against his $1.25-$1.35 trillion range: overvalued at the rumored price. Main risk is AI overreach, magnified by Musk's more than 85% voting control.

notes.title: To a Trillion(s) Dollars and beyond: A SpaceX IPO Odyssey!
notes.text: Base-case intrinsic value $1.22 trillion; simulation median $1.29 trillion across 10,000 runs (no per-share value; cash and debt ignored). Not a buy at the rumored $1.75 trillion IPO price: "one big correction away from being fairly priced or even cheap," and he would then buy. 2025 revenue about $15.6 billion (launch about $4.1 billion, Starlink and related about $11.4 billion, xAI subscriptions about $100 million); estimated EBITDA $8 billion; cost of capital 8%. Musk owns about 42% of equity and about 80% of the votes. At $1.25 trillion EV: about 80x sales and 156x EBITDA. Segment assumptions: launch market $30 billion growing to $100 billion by 2036, share falling from over 80% to 70%, margin 40%; Starlink internet market $15 billion to $160 billion, share 75%, margin near 60% (about 10,000 satellites and over 10 million subscribers at end-2025); xAI 2036 revenue $80 billion at a 50% margin; expansion options $50 billion of revenue at a 30% margin after 2032. Calls the 8% cost of capital reasonable because the risk is company-specific and two-sided.

stocks.summary: His valuation was about $1.22 trillion enterprise value ($1.3 trillion equity, about $100 a share), so not a buy at the rumored $1.75 trillion IPO price and the $1.8-2 trillion listing in June 2026. He would buy only if market cap fell to $1 trillion. He criticizes the $22 trillion xAI addressable-market claim and Musk's voting control, and does not expect index inclusion to change the price.

Facts: first-half revenue about 14x the prior year, operating loss above $8 billion before adjustments, $80 billion reported loss including a $72 billion non-cash charge, compute costs down from over 250% to 48% of quarterly revenue. His worst case is -$373 billion and best case $4.04 trillion; calls both extremes "possible, but unlikely."

notes.title: Faith, Feedback and Fear: Ready for the Valeant Test?
notes.text: Value about $32.50 vs a price near $15 on Nov 8 and just under $14 on Nov 9 (his May 2016 estimate was $43.56, when he bought at $27). A mature, slow-growth pharma company that can no longer grow by acquisition; flat revenue, margins below history; about 87% of the fall in operating income came from amortization and impairments. "I doubled my Valeant holdings."

notes.title: DCF Myth 3.1: The Margin of Safety - Tool for Action or Excuse for Inaction?
notes.text: Bought at $32 when his value was about $45; asks whether he would have bought at a $35 value. Has never used a formal margin of safety; has held off on investments 25% or more undervalued.

notes.title: DCF Myth 3: You cannot do a valuation, when there is too much uncertainty!
notes.text: Value about $44 a share (April 20 post) vs a price about $12 lower. A shift from acquisition-driven growth to a lower-growth pharma business after the drug-pricing and Philidor concerns; default risk treated as a discrete event.

notes.title: Valeant: Information Vacuums, Management Credibility and Investment Value
notes.text: Value about $43.66 a share ("Dog" scenario) vs a $32 price. Cost of capital up from 7.52% to 8.29% after Moody's cut to B1; 5% chance of going-concern failure with liquidation at a 25% discount; revenue down about 2%; half of acquisition expenses moved into operating costs, cutting the pre-tax margin from 43.66% to 40.39%. Bought the stock; value depends on the delayed filing, so there is surprise risk.

notes.title: Checkmate or Stalemate? Valeant's Fall from Investing Grace
notes.text: Value $72.10 a share vs $83.64 on Nov 10 (about 14% below price); after the Salix quarters update, $77 (base) or $81 (optimistic margins). Acquisition charges added back on the assumption that acquisitions stop; price rollbacks cut earnings permanently by about 10%; margin toward the industry's about 25.5%; tax rate rising to 20%; 3% growth for ten years; cost of capital 7.52%. Sat on the sidelines: not significantly undervalued, nor a likely zero; never tempted, because of his skepticism of acquisition-driven growth.

notes.title: Checkmate or Stalemate? Valeant's Fall from Investing Grace
notes.text: Value $72.10 vs $83.64 price (~14% overvalued). Acquisition-driven model under pricing/accounting scrutiny. Action: stay on sidelines.

stocks.summary: He valued it at $72.10 vs $83.64 in Nov 2015 (overvalued), then about $44 vs $32 in April 2016 after pricing and Philidor concerns, bought at about $32 in May 2016 and again near $14 after the Nov 2016 crash (value about $32.50). By March 2017 his base case was $13.68 vs about $12 (roughly fair), he calls the earlier purchases mistakes (average cost about $21), and the wash-sale rule blocks realizing the loss.

Sits between Coca-Cola's pure brand play and Apple's multi-advantage model. No trade disclosed.

profile: Aswath Damodaran is a Professor of Finance at NYU's Stern School of Business, where he has taught corporate finance and valuation since 1986. He holds an MBA and PhD from UCLA and is widely known as the 'Dean of Valuation'. He has won Stern's teaching award several times and was voted most popular business school professor in a 2011 Business Week poll.

He wrote the standard texts Investment Valuation, The Dark Side of Valuation and The Little Book of Valuation, along with Corporate Finance and Investment Fables, and posts his data sets, spreadsheets and class material free on his NYU site. Every January he updates data on country risk, margins, betas and the implied equity risk premium.

Musings on Markets, running since 2008, is where he applies this to live cases: Tesla, Apple, Uber, Nvidia and more recently SpaceX and Anthropic. His method is to tell a story about the business, convert it into revenue, margin and reinvestment assumptions, then compare the resulting value with the market price. He usually discloses whether he bought or sold, and he does not time the market.

purchases.title: Stocks Damodaran says he has bought or traded
purchases.note: Taken only from what he states in the posts read so far (501 of 686), so older trades are likely missing and a position may have changed since the post. Not a record of his portfolio.

rows.name: Facebook / Meta
rows.detail: Called the 2012 IPO at $36 overvalued, then bought at $18 about three months later; bought again at $133 after the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and kept it. Still holds.

rows.name: Microsoft
rows.detail: Bought in 2014 and has held since; kept it through his 2020 and 2022 "mildly overvalued" calls.

rows.name: Alphabet
rows.detail: Said in 2022 he had never held it; by Oct 2026 he says he holds it (and criticizes its dual-class shares).

rows.name: Amazon
rows.detail: Has bought and sold it four times in twenty years; was not an owner from 2012 to 2018, added it back in 2022, and holds it in Oct 2026.

rows.name: JPMorgan Chase
rows.detail: Owned it for nearly a decade; would not sell and would not rush to buy at then-current prices.

rows.name: Citigroup
rows.detail: Said he will add it to his portfolio, though not on price alone.

rows.name: Intel
rows.detail: Valued it at $23.70 a share, undervalued, and said he is buying it, partly to pair with his remaining Nvidia stake.

rows.name: BYD
rows.detail: His limit buy under $80 triggered on April 7, 2025; he calls it a stock he likes.

rows.name: Tencent
rows.detail: Chose Tencent over Alibaba and bought the ADR on Aug 31, 2021, rather than Naspers, to avoid the holding-company discount.

rows.name: Uber
rows.detail: Bought at about $30 after valuing it at $35.42.

rows.name: Levi Strauss
rows.detail: Bought at $18.96 after the IPO.

rows.name: Valeant Pharmaceuticals
rows.detail: Bought at about $32 in May 2016 and again near $14 (average cost about $21); in Nov 2016 "I doubled my Valeant holdings." Calls the purchases mistakes in Mar 2017 but holds at roughly fair value.

rows.name: Twitter
rows.detail: Limit orders executed at about $27 in Aug 2015 and a purchase at $25 late in 2015; by Feb 2016 he was inclined to sell unless the narrative changed.

rows.name: Volkswagen
rows.detail: Invested after his October 2015 valuation.

rows.name: Vale
rows.detail: Already owned it and planned to add in Nov 2014 ($19.40 value vs $8.53); by Sept 2015 his post concluded he should sell.

rows.name: Lukoil
rows.detail: Planned to buy in Nov 2014 and held it near fair value in Apr 2015.

rows.name: Yahoo
rows.detail: Held it for its Alibaba and Yahoo Japan stakes; his 2016 post says he bought after valuing it as a "Walking Dead" company.

rows.name: GE
rows.detail: Said he will buy GE, expecting no dividends until debt is paid down.

rows.name: Beyond Meat
rows.detail: Tried to short at $142 (failed) and bought $120-strike puts expiring Dec 20, 2019.

rows.name: Apple
rows.detail: Held 2010-2012 and sold in April 2012; bought again at $500 (2013) and in 2015, sold at about $220 in Sept 2018, and sold again Aug 19, 2020 when the market cap crossed $2 trillion. Said in 2022 he does not own it.

rows.name: Tesla
rows.detail: Bought in 2019 after a price drop (his "corporate teenager") and sold in January 2020 at $640 (split-adjusted). A 2025 post says he sold his position in the April tariff selloff and was fully exited by May 2025.

rows.name: Nvidia
rows.detail: Bought in 2018 as undervalued; it became a "twenty-bagger." Cut to a quarter of the position in April-May 2025 and sold the rest in four installments, the last in 2026, with no regrets.

rows.name: Palantir
rows.detail: Holds a limit buy not yet reached (Apr-May 2025); interested in owning it "at the right price."

rows.name: MercadoLibre
rows.detail: Holds a limit buy not yet reached (Apr-May 2025); on his buy list in July 2025.

rows.name: SpaceX

profile: John Huber is the portfolio manager and managing member of Saber Capital Management, a value-focused firm in North Carolina that runs separate client accounts and a partnership modeled on Buffett's 1950s partnerships. The accounts have no lockups, and Saber manages nearly all of Huber's own investable capital and most of his family's net worth.

Base Hit Investing is his Substack, an extension of his personal investing journal, with tens of thousands of subscribers. It mixes stock write-ups with thinking on portfolio management, ROIC and behavior. Free posts cover some ideas; paid posts carry the full archive and company research. He says it is educational, not a recommendation service.

Approach: patient, long-term value investing in high-quality businesses bought below their worth, with a heavy focus on free cash flow yield, return on invested capital, buybacks and capital allocation. 'Saber' and 'Base Hit' are baseball metaphors from sabermetrics: get on base steadily rather than swing for home runs.

profile: Praetorian Capital Fund is a concentrated, long-biased hedge fund run by founder and CIO Harris Kupperman. It began investing on January 1, 2019 and writes quarterly letters to investors.

How it invests: a core book of a handful of concentrated, asymmetric positions (typically at least 5% of capital each, mostly companies worth $1-5 billion, never above 5% of a company), plus an Event-Driven book of shorter situations. Its themes are inflation and fiscal stress ('Project Zimbabwe'), a weaker US dollar and emerging markets, precious metals, uranium, offshore energy and refiners. It avoids large-cap tech and expects most AI capital to be impaired.

Fund facts from the letters: about $343 million of net assets at March 2024 and about $350 million with 198 investors at September 2024; a 1.25% management fee and a 20% incentive allocation; a Cayman offshore vehicle. Returns are unaudited estimates.

blogs.coverage: All 39 quarterly letters read (Q1 2017 through Q3 2026), from the PDFs on the fund's partnership page. The letters rarely give tickers, so I added tickers from general knowledge and a few may be wrong; baskets and unlisted or OTC names have no chart link. Letters dated 2019-2026 show only the month they were posted (the 1st), not the exact day. Unnamed positions are not covered.
profile: Alluvial Capital Management is a registered investment adviser run by Dave Waters, CFA, from Pittsburgh (later Sewickley), Pennsylvania. It began in 2014, and the flagship Alluvial Fund, LP started on January 1, 2017. The fund is audited by Cohen & Company, and Waters has said his family's investable assets are entirely in it.

How it invests: a concentrated, deep-value approach focused on small and micro-cap companies that large funds cannot own, often illiquid, post-bankruptcy or OTC 'expert market' names, plus special situations (liquidations, spin-offs, merger arbitrage). Early letters favored rural telecoms, hotels, bank special situations and coal; later holdings broadened to Italian and Swedish fiber, Polish small caps, ECIP community banks, post-reorganization energy and offshore services.

The same pattern recurs: Waters buys at single-digit earnings or deep discounts to asset value, holds while management returns cash or sells, and sells on governance or valuation concerns. A sister Tactile Fund, planned for 2025, targets companies with extraordinary physical assets.

notes.text: Top-5. The CEO resigned unexpectedly in early May and shares fell over 20%; he added substantially. A 'good co / bad co': the first facility ran at about 50% gross margin, the second (built on spec) dragged consolidated margins negative. Fiscal Q4 (April year-end) showed gross margin back to 20% and positive cash flow, plus positive guidance, so shares re-rated; he now calls it 'good co / good co'. Outside politicians' crosshairs; capacity could double again, financed with customer funding; revenue could triple guidance in 4-5 years.

notes.title: Q1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Recession-proof biologics maker with very high switching costs (the manufacturing site is named in the FDA drug application), cited as the template for the Recro idea.

notes.title: H1 2018 Letter to Partners

The drug-development arm was sold off, removing the 'eminent domain' worry that a customer's manufacturing capacity could be reclaimed. Biologics are enormously complex (aspirin has 21 atoms, a biologic may have 25,000), giving high barriers and switching costs; the plant ran at about 50% capacity, so operating leverage is large. Presented at Value X Vail by Adam Patinkin of David Capital Partners.

stocks.summary: Contract manufacturer of large-molecule biologics and held since 2018 (first named as CDMO). He saw capacity expansion filling to roughly $100-125M of free cash flow and valued it at 20x. It was his largest 2023 loser (shares halved on guidance, with a convertible due 2026), then sold to two private equity firms in early 2025 at a price he considered disappointing.

notes.title: H1 2022 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Q1 2022 Letter to Partners

notes.title: YE 2021 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: growing SaaS alongside Yellow Pages cash flow; the overhang from a distressed investor's (Mudrick) sale, partly to the CEO and Chairman, is temporary.

notes.title: H1 2021 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Q1 2021 Letter to Partners

stocks.summary: A former Yellow Pages company turning into small-business SaaS, held from 2021. The legacy business funds growth while SaaS overtakes it (about mid-2025). Shares have fallen several times (a distressed seller, then a 2025 guidance trim); he calls about 9x FY26 SaaS EBITDA absurd and notes repeated insider buying. By the YE 2025 letter he had exited, calling it a likely mistake because its distribution advantage was finite and management credibility impaired.

stocks.name: Iteris

notes.title: Q1 2021 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held 5+ years: the board rejected a $8.15-$8.50 takeover proposal and is running a sale process; shares about 25% below the bid; he expects $9-$12 and a close within 6-12 months.

notes.title: H1 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: exited agriculture to become a cash-flow-positive intelligent traffic control company; expects operating leverage past $200M of revenue and would favor a sale if the board fails to deliver.

notes.title: March 2020 Interim Update
notes.text: Traffic management company with no debt and a cash-rich balance sheet. Customer purchases may slip a few months, but it has led its market for 30 years and plans to buy smaller players, which should be more vulnerable than Iteris. It is at the front of replacing analog traffic monitoring with SaaS/cloud products, a shift that has been glacial because of municipal customers; he suggests that virus-driven work-from-home needs might speed adoption.

notes.title: YE 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-6. About 50% share of traffic sensors; a new CFO with an operational IT background and two new directors; he hopes the board will exit agriculture to become a pure-play intelligent-transportation company, focus on ROIC and announce a strategic relaunch. Transportation should grow low double digits organically, faster with bolt-on M&A.

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Named among the defensive holdings: mostly long-term contracts, and traffic is not a problem that is going away.

notes.title: H1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Strong performer year to date: the estate of the largest holder has fully exited; a June bolt-on acquisition lets it cross-sell software into new geographies, putting shares at a mid-teens multiple of traffic free cash flow. CEO Joe Bergera is a Roper veteran and he sees Iteris as a platform for Roper-style niche M&A. He criticizes the board for raising equity (selling 18% of traffic and 18% of agriculture rather than just selling all of agriculture), likening it to an over-indulgent parent raiding the college fund for acting lessons, but thinks the deal still adds value and expects high-teens revenue growth with operating leverage.

notes.title: Q1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5 for over three years. Cisco smart-city partnership announced; touch point with a third of U.S. signalized intersections. Lloyd Miller's estate sold about 2.5M shares at a discount, taking its stake from over 15% to below 5% and removing an overhang. A recent peer deal at 4.7x sales implies about $15 a share with agriculture at zero; potential acquirers include E&C firms (ACM, JEC), telecoms (VZ, CMCSA) and big-data companies (CSCO, GOOG). He now concedes the upside scenarios for agriculture are off the table, yet $0 is also wrong, and strategic options for it are likely. Combined GAAP reporting makes the stock screen badly.

notes.title: YE 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Ended the year with about a 75% gain since initiation but fell nearly 50% in 2018, mostly in Q1, with the largest holder's estate selling. He added significantly: the business looks like consulting, government BPO and asset-light project management (high-teens to low-20s cash-flow multiples), 2018 one-time items roll off, and peer deals suggest multiples of the current price. The venture-stage agriculture business could alone exceed the market cap.

notes.title: Q1 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Fell about 30% in Q1 and 10% more in early Q2; he added significantly. Reasons: (1) demoted to subcontractor on a Virginia DOT contract that was rolled into a bigger one with unattractive services (road-side assistance, rest stops); (2) Texas mix shift and a centralized procurement team weighing on margins; (3) owner Lloyd Miller (about 15%) died and his estate is selling; (4) quant and technical selling. He sees the transportation businesses alone as justifying the price, and agriculture alone at about $250M versus a ~$150M EV, with a new president who has seen four employers sold.

notes.title: YE 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Still materially undervalued; leads development of smart infrastructure for autonomous cars. A sale of agriculture seems likely and could alone justify over half the market cap. The stock fell over 30% high to low in one month in Q4.

notes.title: Q3 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5. The agriculture/weather unit was moved into a separate entity and a new head, Jim Chambers, has had four companies he worked at get acquired, so a sale of agriculture seems likely, although the company also signaled it might raise cash. The traffic business is an 'undiscovered gem' for intelligent transportation and autonomous vehicles.

notes.title: H1 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Five separate drops of 15% or more in six months, yet the stock returned 76%. Transportation operating income rose from $11.7M (FY16) to $18.3M (FY17), implying over $12M of free cash flow (vs. the $8M in the marketing materials), so agriculture is free. Iteris leads the development of the ARC-IT architecture for the U.S. Department of Transportation and is the leading intersection-sensor supplier, positioning it for autonomous vehicles. Agriculture enterprise sales slipped to 2019; it was put in a separate legal entity, hinting at an eventual sale. He added to the position.

notes.title: YE 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Up about 66% in 2016. The traffic businesses are executing well and the agriculture 'lotto ticket', valued at zero when bought, is reaching an inflection point and could be worth multiples of the original investment.

notes.title: Q2 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Bought at about $2.19 a share (market cap about $70M, too small for institutions and showing GAAP losses). 'Good co / bad co': two growing, cash-generating Intelligent Transportation businesses that he valued at $4 a share alone, plus a money-losing agricultural weather-analytics unit that he got for less than free. All that is needed is for management to shut agriculture if it fails; the CEO holds 1.35M options and activist Lloyd Miller owns 15.6%. If agriculture works, the investment could rise over 500%. He presented it at ValueX Vail (slide deck attached to the letter).

notes.title: Iteris presentation, Value X Vail 2016
notes.text: 2016 Value X Vail deck on a 'good co / bad co' nano-cap (price $2.59 on 6/17/2016, 32.0M shares, market cap ~$83M, cash $16.0M, no debt, EV ~$67M, insiders 5.2%, 52-week range $1.67-2.65). Two cash-generating transportation businesses (Roadway Sensors and Transportation Systems consulting) are hidden by a money-losing agriculture analytics unit: for the twelve months to March 2016 segment operating income was $7.7M for Sensors and $4.0M for Systems, versus a $7.4M loss in Analytics. Management believed the two core businesses would produce about $8M of free cash flow standalone; headcount rose from 300 to 450 and R&D was up 126% since 2013. It screens poorly: the 2014 10-K was delayed by revenue-recognition problems, one-time audit, consulting and severance costs, and a $10.1M deferred-tax valuation allowance obscure results. Transportation: Sensors revenue 12% CAGR (up 11% YoY), Systems up 7%, backlog $63.3M up 61%; about 65% of sensor sales upgrade old inductive loops to camera-based smart intersections; a $140B annual cost of congestion. Sensors is fragmented without a moat but is taking share (double-digit growth versus about 7% for the industry). The 'lotto ticket' is its role keeping the U.S. DOT connected-vehicle reference architecture. Valuation: $8M free cash flow at 10x gives $3.00 a share (+16%); a go-forward $7M at 14-18x gives $3.56-4.43 (+37% to +71%). Agriculture (ClearAg): SaaS weather and agronomy analytics, 18 patents with 28 pending, 5 of the top 10 crop-science firms signed, not first (Climate Corp sold to Monsanto for $1B, Weather Corp to IBM for $2B). Capturing 4% of 2.1M farms at $1,200 gives $100M of sales; at 3-5x sales that is $3.00-$5.00 a share of extra value, so Ag implies $5.56 to $19.60 versus $4.00 for the core alone. Not needed for the thesis; if Ag fails, cut after a reasonable period (2019?) and transportation should be worth $5+. Risks: management attached to Ag (mitigant: activist Lloyd Miller owns 15.6%), low insider ownership (new CEO has 1.35M options, CFO bought in the open market), Waze-type disruption, government budgets. Repurchased $5.2M of stock since 2011.

stocks.summary: Intelligent traffic management company held for more than five years until at least 2021; the board rejected a $8.15-$8.50 offer and ran a sale process, with Sweeney expecting $9-$12.

notes.title: H1 2026 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Q1 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: the strategic review ended without a sale and event-driven holders sold; he sees buyers above the price and upside from a new CEO; Catalent's sale to Novo Holdings should push fill-finish customers elsewhere; expects index funds to buy about 20 days of volume on joining the Russell 2000.

notes.title: Q1 2023 Letter to Partners

notes.title: YE 2022 Letter to Partners

notes.title: H1 2022 Letter to Partners

notes.text: Exited: still likes the business but was uneasy about valuation and convertible-debt refinancing risk.

notes.title: H1 2025 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Q1 2025 Letter to Partners

notes.title: YE 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held (top 5): now a pure-play restaurant software company after selling Defense; management expects about 25% growth with flat operating expenses for two years, which he thinks yields substantial FCF.

notes.title: Q1 2024 Letter to Partners

notes.title: H1 2021 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Q1 2021 Letter to Partners

notes.title: YE 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: dominant restaurant POS software with a clear growth path, though valuation is not cheap.

notes.title: Q3 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Still a top-5 position and the roadmap for the Cantaloupe investment: restaurant POS software, formerly mismanaged until activist pressure put Savneet Singh in charge, who rebuilt the culture around ROIC and best-in-class software; the stock is up 4x since he took over. notes.title: H1 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: cloud POS for fast-casual and quick-serve restaurants; he expects chains to gain share from independents and M&A to accelerate given its balance sheet.

notes.title: March 2020 Interim Update

Technology is best in breed, a new CEO has laid out a plan to add capabilities and lift revenue per user, and a recent convertible bond leaves it flush with cash. If the industry slows, acquisitions may become cheaper, letting PAR speed up its product plans.

notes.title: YE 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-6, a relative newcomer: a mid-sized position after a convertible offering fortified the balance sheet. He knew it from friends Voss Capital and ADW Capital, who helped recruit CEO Savneet Singh. Value centers on Brink, the cloud restaurant POS; more doors and 4-5x ARPU over several years; customers are quick-service and fast-casual restaurants that trade down in recessions.

stocks.summary: Restaurant and convenience-store software (POS, back office, loyalty via Punchh) held since 2020. Not cheap, but he liked its competitive position, Ron Shaich's $160M investment and later the pure-play shape after selling its Defense unit. Still held in Q3 2025 with a record backlog and delayed rollouts; he blamed a sharp share fall on AI-driven software multiple compression, then exited in Q1 2026 over valuation and convertible-debt refinancing risk.
