notes.title: YE 2022 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held. It traded at a discount to its cash and the discount widened, so it did not work as a hedge.

notes.title: H1 2022 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Long-term holding expected to receive about C$6.00 a share from a PLM sale, lifting cash to about C$575M against a ~C$400M market cap; portfolio ballast.

notes.title: Q1 2022 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: agreed to sell its PLM stake to Aeromexico for C$5.58 a share in cash; plans to return $75M through buybacks and expand disclosure on other investments.

notes.title: YE 2021 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5 long-term holding. He expects AeroMexico to buy PLM for about $375M plus adjustments, leaving over C$6 a share in cash; Trade X grows 300-400% a year and could be worth more than Aimia's whole EV; more Kognitiv disclosure expected.

notes.title: H1 2021 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top holding. New management is monetizing assets, mainly the ~50% PLM stake that may be sold to AeroMexico near the $400M or 7.5x EBITDA floor; Clear Media expected to be worth 2-3x Aimia's cost; Kognitiv a likely SPAC target; airlines owning loyalty programs (Air Canada/Aeroplan) are valued higher.

notes.title: YE 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held. Now a lean holding company; he thinks the most valuable asset, PLM (bankruptcy-remote), is not in the share price. AeroMexico expected to emerge with Apollo as largest shareholder.

notes.title: H1 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held and added to as new management cuts costs, moves loyalty assets off balance sheet (Kognitiv merger, about C$1.80 a share) and pursues a dividend recap at PLM. About two-thirds of market cap is cash; he cites a sell-side target of C$9.50. PLM (49%, AeroMexico loyalty) has a $400M floor via AeroMexico's option at 7.5x EBITDA; AeroMexico's bankruptcy is a risk. Clear Media (a former LWC holding) is also in its portfolio.

notes.title: March 2020 Interim Update
notes.text: Called a box of cash plus a near-50% interest in Aeromexico's loyalty program PLM, which is bankruptcy-remote from Aeromexico. Shares fell hard, but the cash buys more and Aimia's position against Aeromexico likely improved, since Aeromexico's core airline business will suffer from the drop in air travel. That could let Aimia extract value from PLM via financial engineering, such as a dividend recap or an extended PLM contract. He believed Aimia's value had gone up over the prior few weeks despite the lower price.

notes.title: YE 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: One of six rotating top positions. A new board takes over in March 2020. He sees Aeromexico's earlier bid for the ~50% PLM stake as an attempt to exploit an incompetent board rather than a valuation signpost; PLM is recession-resistant and key to Aeromexico, whose contract runs through 2030, and Aimia needs PLM to avoid PFIC designation, so a sale is unlikely soon. Air Canada has had operational problems integrating Aeroplan. The cash is in the hands of allocators with strong records, expenses will be cut, and he does not expect the cash to go into Mittleman's own portfolio.

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Top-10 holding, described as a cash shell: a dollar is worth more than a dollar in a downturn. He expected a broad management overhaul and paid a fraction of asset value. Cited as a stock punished for near-term cloudiness.

notes.title: H1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5. A cash shell with a money-losing loyalty business and valuable investments; NAV $6-9. The board owns about 0% of the stock; shareholders called a special meeting and Mittleman Brothers (largest holder; standstill expired) is expected to propose a new slate; the company is aggressively repurchasing. He argues Mittleman will assemble capital allocators to buy controlling stakes in operating businesses, not just a vehicle for its own holdings (the PFIC tax issue rules that out), emphasizing stable current cash flows (two-thirds of Mittleman's holdings saw no FCF/EBITDA decline in the financial crisis).

notes.title: Q1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Now top-5, and the recipient of two public letters (made public) calling for board members to step down; afterward the chairman and one director resigned, and he expects the board to be replaced at the AGM or in a July proxy contest. Management plans a venture-capital-style acquisition strategy in loyalty, which he opposes. With cash greater than market cap, no debt, preferred dividends covered by distributions from a ~50% stake in Club Premier (Aeromexico), the International Loyalty Solutions business, a ~$64M stake in Cardlytics, a 20% stake in BIG Loyalty (AirAsia), about $800M of tax assets and a tender offer for about 25% of shares, he sees essentially zero downside. He says small-company boards have little oversight because proxy fights cost hundreds of thousands or millions.

notes.title: Q3 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Now mid-sized (first bought some time ago, a loyalty idea from researching Points.com). Air Canada ended its Aeroplan deal for 2020; Mittleman Brothers (about 18%) is an activist. A consortium (Air Canada, TD, CIBC, Visa) bid C$250M for Aeroplan (about $1.60 a share, plus about $2 of other value) and he increased the position because the bid was far too low: 2% interchange economics, Air Canada's own $2B valuation of a loyalty program, about 5M members (acquiring 40% would cost about $300M in sign-up miles alone), and Air Canada trading at a discount for lacking a captive program. Air Canada raised the bid 80% to C$450M, a quick return. After closing, Aimia becomes cash, a large NOL and assorted loyalty assets; he guesses NAV of $6-10 a share and expects debt paydown, preferred dividends, buybacks or acquisitions under Mittleman.

stocks.summary: Canadian holding company whose main assets were a ~49% stake in PLM (AeroMexico's loyalty program, with a $400M floor from AeroMexico's option), plus Kognitiv, Trade X and Clear Media. Sweeney held it from 2020 as a top position at a large discount to cash, expecting about C$6 a share of cash from a PLM sale. By late 2022 the discount had widened and it had not worked as a hedge.

stocks.name: EZCorp

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Being sold, and the mistake explained. A 3,000-year-old business model, recession-proof, with very high incremental margins on loans. Controlling shareholder Phil Cohen owned about 6% but 100% of the vote and had taken $6-7M a year of consulting fees until the arrangement ended, and a new CEO came in after the 'eBay of pawn' detour, acquisition write-downs and kitchen-sinking. Pawn economics: loan-to-value is effectively COGS on forfeited items; lending at 80 cents versus 60 is pure profit. The stock was bought at about 1x EBIT and rose, but the convertible bond was a warning: markets and banks priced Cohen's controlled company at about 12% versus ~6% for First Cash. He ignored that message because of counter-cyclicality and gold. Just before the meeting an 8-K said Cohen would become Chairman and pay himself about $3M a year (First Cash's chairman gets about $250K), acquisitions grew too expensive and he would not repurchase non-voting shares. EZPW traded near 7x normalized free cash flow versus about 30x for First Cash, yet he decided to exit.

notes.title: H1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Fell out of the top 5 as defensive names were sized up; still mid-sized. Recession-proof business at the depths of its cycle with a very low cash-flow valuation and below break-up value; governance improved (board revamped, pay tied to per-share metrics); a digital initiative could attract fintech investors.

notes.title: EZCorp presentation, MOI Best Ideas 2019
notes.text: Best Ideas 2019 deck (EZPW at $7.73 on 12/31/2018; ~54.6M shares, market cap ~$422M, cash ~$286M including securities and the receivable, debt ~$316M, EV ~$575M, insiders 10.6%, 52-week range $7.45-15.10). Pitch: a recession-proof, cash-flowing, growing business at multiples not seen since 2008 and a 50%+ discount to peers. FY18: 508 U.S. stores (80% of net revenue, segment EBITDA $116M, 30.6% margin) and 454 Latin American stores (20%, $38.4M, 39.5%); Latin America store count grew 84% in 2018 with 22-44% growth guided for 2019 (100-200 stores). Pawn: more than 3 in 5 Mexicans unbanked, maintenance capex about 1% of gross revenue, Mexico has 7,000+ stores and 22 operators with 50+ stores. Operations: 18 straight quarters of constant-currency same-store pawn-loan growth in Latin America and growth in 11 of 12 quarters in the U.S.; through the Great Recession EBITDA grew from $65M to $192M with revenue up 22-31% a year. Near-term upside is baked in: the 2017 hurricanes cost ~$6.9M of 2018 EBITDA, a full year of 2018 acquisitions adds ~$6.2M, so 2019 base adjusted EBITDA could be ~$113.6M (+13%) with no operational improvement. Self-financing capacity of $90-105M for acquisitions at an expected 25% ROIC. New LatAm stores earn ~12% monthly yield and ~$138k net revenue per store versus ~18% and ~$240k for legacy stores. Why mispriced: the May 2018 convertible (2025 notes at $15.90) triggered convert-arb shorting, dilution fears and a ~50% price drop with no follow-on acquisition (he views the convert as equity sold at 11.4x EBITDA, while acquisitions were done at about 4.8x), plus tax-loss selling after a ~100% run; AMLO's election in Mexico raised regulation fears he calls unfounded (government has run a pawn network since 1774); 27 Canadian payday stores drag EBITDA by ~$3.8M. Hidden assets (~17% of the price): a ~35% Cash Converters stake (about $0.63 a share) and the Alpha/Grupo Finmart receivable (~$37M present value, ~$30M expected in 2019). Cohen: 5.5% of stock, 100% of the vote, discount to FCFS now historically wide (the FCFS EV/EBITDA premium is above 100%, versus a 15-year average of 31-44%); CEO Grimshaw will sell shares via 10b5-1 to buy a home. Valuation: NAV $6.79-13.14 a share (middle $11.13, +44%); financial-crisis multiple of 5.0x on 'normal' EBITDA of $117.9M gives $7.61 (-2%); normal EBITDA at current multiple $9.16 (+18%), at 15-year comp discount $14.32 (+85%), at the pre-acquisition discount $16.14 (+109%); 2020 with 600 LatAm stores $19.20 (+148%) and 2021 with 725 stores $20.70 (+168%). FCFS is a logical buyer. Risks: controlling shareholder, convert dependence, regulation, retail weakness, universal basic income.

notes.title: YE 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Stock fell about 35% in 2018 despite exceptional operations. He presented it at the Manual of Ideas Best Ideas Conference in January (deck attached). Cash-flowing, growing, recession-proof and below net asset value; negatives are a controlling shareholder who has not always looked after minorities, offset by recent governance changes, one-time costs rolling off in 2019, a clear growth plan, and a convert (May 2018) whose dilution only starts after about a 100% rally. He added near the Q4 low and also earlier near asset value, and calls the latter a mistake (he should have built in more margin of safety).

notes.title: Q3 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Frustrating after the May 2018 convertible (conversion price $15.90). He argues shares outstanding have grown only about 2% a year over 30 years, and an all-stock acquisition at $15.90 (about 9x EBITDA vs 4-5x for acquisitions) would have been called accretive. He inferred from a plane crash in Honduras (tail number tracked) that executives had visited Colombia and an acquisition may be pending. A new three-year plan is coming, probably tying pay to per-share metrics after shareholder pressure from him and larger holders. A lapping of last year's hurricane season, cyclical weakness from record-low unemployment and a very low valuation set a low bar.

notes.title: H1 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5 since inception. Latin American store count almost doubled and EBITDA more than doubled in a year, financed by low-coupon converts. The convert dilutes equity (so he lowered his long-term target) and EZPW is an 'orphan' stock (dual class puts off institutions, not sexy for growth investors, converts worry value investors); there is a Catch-22 in 2024 when the converts mature, since the company would repurchase stock it issued cheaply. Near term he likes the arbitrage-driven selling, the cash for accretive acquisitions (several small ones announced), and operating leverage in Latin America. Updated deck was in the Q2 2017 letter.

notes.title: YE 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5. Second-largest public pawn operator. In 2017 management greatly improved store-level performance, strengthened the balance sheet and returned to acquisitive growth, yet the stock was a negative contributor until mid-November and lagged for the year. He says it should anchor the portfolio when the economy softens.

notes.title: Q3 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5. He puts the convertible-bond weakness behind it, now that the company bought 112 Latin American stores. The narrative should shift to growth after a 3-year plan, and he thinks FirstCash will realize that the best move is to buy EZCorp at a premium, since it could cut nearly all its infrastructure and would otherwise face competitive bids for every other pawn group.

notes.title: H1 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Stock fell substantially in H1 despite strong execution (he attributes it to non-economic selling from portfolio positioning and tax strategy). He presented it at Value X Vail in late June (deck posted on the firm site). On June 28 EZCorp announced a debt refinancing via a convertible bond and a possible Latin American acquisition. The convert caused a sharp sell-off, partly arbitrage shorting; he lowered his upside targets and his faith in management's stewardship of equity, but kept near-term upside above 100% and multi-bagger potential via renewed growth and an eventual end to the dual share structure. He calls it a defensive business and withheld final judgment until the acquisition details.

notes.title: EZCorp presentation, Value X Vail 2017
notes.text: June 2017 deck (EZPW at $8.95 on 6/20/17; 54.3M shares, market cap ~$486M, cash $120M, debt $280M, EV ~$531M, insiders 8.2%, 52-week range $6.66-12.00). Second-largest public pawn operator (IPO 1991): 517 U.S. stores (88% of net revenue, segment EBITDA $114M, 31% margin) and 239 Mexico stores (12%, $13.5M EBITDA), plus a tiny Canadian payday operation. New CEO Stuart Grimshaw (left the CEO job at Australia's third-largest bank) with former CEO Joe Rotunda back as COO. Pawn is an essential service (about one in four Americans under- or unbanked; average customer ~36 years old, ~$29,000 income; average loan ~$150, ~84% redeemed; 80% use pawn more than twice a year), secured lending, low capex, about 3,000 years old; U.S. has 10,000+ stores and FCFS and EZPW ~1,600 combined, Mexico ~1,200 combined. Mispriced because of an unsavory industry, controlling shareholder Philip Cohen (5.5% of stock, 100% of the vote; consulting fees via Madison Park in 2011-13, terminated in 2014, and a Delaware ruling in January 2016 applying 'entire fairness' makes a repeat unlikely, so share price is his only path to wealth), a 3-year plan that obscures earnings power, and hidden assets. Stock rose ~300% in 2016 then fell ~35% on portfolio-sizing and tax-driven selling. Plan: step 1 clean house (write-offs, divestments, inventory reset); step 2 back to basics, growing pawn loans (6 straight U.S. quarters of growth, 7 of double-digit Mexico growth), new POS and store-level incentives; step 3 cut costs (corporate expense target $50M in 2018 versus $68M in 2016, store-level savings such as turning assistant managers into lead pawnbrokers, roughly $7M estimated) and refinance (2016 effective rates of 14% on the term loan and 8% on the cash converts, versus FCFS at 5.375%; hypothetical payoff worth $3.34-4.11 a share). Management equity awards vest three years later with 80% EBITDA / 20% net debt targets, rewarding a lean 2018. Reinvestment: de novo Mexico stores cost ~$320k with a ~3-year payback; 500 Mexican stores in five years could be worth $460-552M EBITDA-based, roughly today's EV. Hidden assets worth ~23% of the share price: a 31% Cash Converters stake (about $0.76 a share) and a Grupo Finmart note (sold for $50M plus a $91M note, $25M due 2H17, $26M in 2018, $18M in 2019). Regulation risk overstated (no major change in 25 years; four states raised rates recently; payday is the real problem). Valuation: zero-growth 6% DCF gives ~$647M (+33%); NAV of stores, cash, Cash Converters and notes less debt is $7.90-14.28 a share (EZPW at a 13% discount to a middle case and FCFS at a ~75% premium to NAV); consensus 2018 EBITDA of $104M at 8-10x gives $12.02-15.74 (+34% to +76%); LWC 'normal' EBITDA $114M plus cash accumulation and notes gives $16.38-20.46 (+83% to +129%); a strategic buyer with $35M of synergies could pay $24.78-30.27. The controlling holder is about 68 and a sale to FCFS is likely eventually. Risks: regulation, controlling shareholder, weaker retail or online shift, universal basic income.

notes.title: Seeking Alpha PRO interview (April 2017)
notes.text: Called one of his highest-conviction ideas. The stock rallied over 300% from low to high in 2016, then heavy tax-motivated selling in early 2017 created non-economic negative momentum. Controlling shareholder is not always friendly to minorities, but the company cleaned up operations, is taking share from its largest competitor, has room to reinvest through consolidation and de novo stores, and traded below 8x trailing free cash flow. He says sell-side analysts value it on current earnings while admitting these are not normal. Looking out a few years it could earn $1-$2 a share and deserves a higher multiple given the friendlier regulatory climate. The controlling holder was 67, and he thought First Cash (at 19x earnings) would jump at the largest remaining pawn operator, implying $20-40 a share in a takeout within a few years. Recession-proof, with liquidation value not far below the price.

notes.title: YE 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Best performer of 2016 (about +250%). Recession-proof and still cheap on normalized free cash flow, with meaningful cost cuts announced and growth in the U.S. and Latin America resuming. He calls it the most attractive collection of pawn assets for an aggressive acquirer, with an aging controlling shareholder.

notes.title: Q1 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Bought on launch day at $2.89 (market cap about $158M, EV about $477M); the shares had lost $1.59 in 2015 and filing was delayed by a Mexican vs U.S. GAAP error. Sum of the parts: Cash Converters (32% stake, about $60M, $1.09 a share); Grupo Finmart (payroll-advance lender that lost $22M, with $159M of non-recourse debt EZPW can walk away from); Mexican pawn (237 stores, worth about $60M at about $250K a store based on First Cash's purchases, or $1.09 a share); and U.S. pawn (522 stores, $80M segment EBIT, implied at only 2.5x EBIT, about $383K a store versus $960K-$1.4M paid in recent deals). At 10x segment EBIT the shares are worth $11.66 and at 15x almost $19; a financial buyer might pay $9-10. Joe Rotunda (CEO 2000-2010) is back running U.S. pawn; Stuart Grimshaw's option package ties him to the share price; Phil Cohen (6% owner, all the votes) lost a $6M-a-year consulting deal. Pawn consolidates (13,000 U.S. shops, 90% independent), is counter-cyclical (revenue nearly doubled 2007-10) and is helped by gold. Beta near 2. Shares were already up over 50% from his purchase price by the letter date.

stocks.summary: Second-largest U.S. pawn operator, a core holding from 2016. Thesis: pawn is recession-proof, trades below net asset value, and the company grows in Latin America. The 2018 convertible and controlling-shareholder governance weighed on the stock.

stocks.name: NextNav

notes.title: H1 2026 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: awaiting an FCC proposed rule; the balance sheet improved after SPAC warrants were called and convertibles converted; the CEO testified before a House subcommittee.

notes.title: Q1 2026 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Outsized position: he believes the FCC's draft rule is advancing through White House review and sees value well above the roughly $15 month-end price; Amazon, Globalstar and SpaceX interest in terrestrial spectrum is positive.

notes.title: YE 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: expects an FCC rulemaking ('when' not 'if') and estimates spectrum near $60 a share in the best case; AT&T bought EchoStar's low-band spectrum, and Verizon, T-Mobile face low-band congestion; Starlink a possible bidder.

notes.title: Q3 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: pending FCC approval to repurpose spectrum for 5G; he cites FCC chair remarks and the AT&T/EchoStar spectrum deal, which implies about $60 a share.

notes.title: H1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5: expects an FCC rulemaking and spectrum monetization with a mobile operator at $35-$60 a share.

notes.title: Q1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Largest position: weakness from venture fund selling and GAAP optics; he expects a possible FCC rulemaking by early fall and values the spectrum at 3-5x the stock price.

notes.title: YE 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Largest position: awaiting FCC action on its 900 MHz petition for terrestrial GPS and about 15 MHz of 5G spectrum; at Verizon's $1.44 per MHz-pop he estimates about $40 a share before any premium; pressure is a temporary fund-selling overhang.

notes.title: H1 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5: owns wireless spectrum and has petitioned the FCC to swap and repurpose it for 5G; $1.00 per MHz-pop would imply about $30 a share (he cites a much lower price at the time); insider Joe Samberg bought.

notes.title: Q1 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Now a large position, added after a discounted acquisition; sees low-band spectrum worth over $20 a share if repurposed.

notes.title: YE 2023 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New position bought at under 30 cents per MHz-pop of spectrum; he expects an FCC request to repurpose spectrum for broadband and cites 2x-7x+ spectrum value comparables (Verizon/Straight Path 2017). Spartacus SPAC merged into it.

stocks.summary: Owns wireless spectrum and a terrestrial GPS alternative; bought from 2023 at under 30 cents per MHz-pop. The thesis is an FCC rulemaking repurposing 900 MHz spectrum for 5G, with Verizon's $1.44 per MHz-pop and the AT&T/EchoStar deal as valuation markers ($40-60 a share). Often his largest position, still held in mid-2026 while awaiting an FCC proposed rule (a draft was moving through White House review).

stocks.name: Vistry Group

notes.title: Q1 2026 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Exited: the CEO's retirement and uncertain buybacks impaired the thesis; he may revisit it.

notes.title: YE 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: about 4.5x 2026 EBIT vs low double-digit transaction comps; buying back shares; could double and still trade below pre-accounting-problem levels.

notes.title: Q3 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: capital-light partnerships model; GBP39B ten-year funding program should drive growth in 2027; about 4.5x 2026 EBIT vs low double-digit transaction comps; CEO bought about GBP1M.

notes.title: H1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5: a new GBP39B government housing program should help H2 2025 and 2026; the $800M operating profit goal is attainable from a price below tangible book.

notes.title: Q1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: thesis intact though slower due to legacy accounting problems and delayed capital returns; insider buying, buybacks and government support for UK affordable housing.

notes.title: YE 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held (top 5): 2024 problems tied to the legacy business being wound down; below tangible book and under 3x his 2025 EBIT (above GBP500M).

notes.title: H1 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5: exiting traditional building for Partnerships and buying back stock; targets GBP800M EBIT, about 4x vs 12-13x in past deals; CEO Greg Fitzgerald bought shares.

notes.title: YE 2023 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: exiting traditional homebuilding to focus on partnerships, with a planned ~GBP1B buyback over three years and a GBP3B+ market cap; multi-bagger potential.

notes.title: H1 2023 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: likes the asset-light Partnerships business with local housing authorities and expects a capital allocation review to lead to aggressive buybacks; cheap alongside the FTSE 100.

notes.title: YE 2022 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: its Partnerships business could earn GBP450M after tax, about 5x current value, with a higher multiple possible. (Countryside Partnerships, a prior holding, was acquired by Vistry in November.)

stocks.summary: UK homebuilder pivoting to an asset-light Partnerships model, held since the Countryside deal in 2022. 2024 accounting problems hit the shares, but he sees it below tangible book and at 3-4.5x EBIT, helped by a new GBP39B ten-year government funding program, a GBP1B buyback and CEO share purchases. He exited in Q1 2026 after the CEO's retirement and uncertain buybacks impaired the thesis.

stocks.name: Cantaloupe (formerly USA Technologies)

notes.title: H1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Taken private by a PE buyer this quarter; solid return but a disappointing price; the chairman rolled his equity.

notes.title: Q1 2025 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held: Reuters reports a sale process; he is unsure it is the right time to sell since operating leverage is just starting; under 3x revenue vs 4-6x for historical sales.

notes.title: YE 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held (top 5): low churn, cash-generative, growing high-teens under new leadership; expects a re-rating.

notes.title: H1 2024 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New position and a repeat holding from 2020-21: about $60M of FCF if the $75M FY2026 EBITDA target is met (mid-to-high single-digit FCF multiple); insiders bought.

notes.title: YE 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Held (as USA Technologies, USAT): unattended retail and vending software under a new board and management cutting costs and focusing on enterprise software; index inclusion expected to help.

notes.title: Q3 2020 Letter to Partners
notes.text: The undisclosed top-5 position from the first-half letter (full write-up sent separately). End-to-end cashless payments and enterprise software for vending and unattended retail; sales are recession-resistant. Best-in-class service, but a history of poor management: five CFOs in rapid succession led to accounting irregularities, late SEC filings and a Nasdaq delisting, and the stock fell from above $15 to below $4 as the delisting forced sales. Competitive position was largely unaffected. Activist Hudson Executive Capital (with other insiders almost 20% of shares) took over; led by Doug Braunstein, former JP Morgan CFO, with chairman Douglas Bergeron (took Verifone from $50M to $5B enterprise value) and CEO Sean Feeney, who focuses on best-in-class SaaS and profitable growth. Easy levers: replacing expensive consultants with employees, and lapping restatement and activist-battle costs. Payments revenue carries single-digit gross margin versus roughly 70% for SaaS, and about half of customers do not use the software, so shifting mix (even with some cannibalization) could multiply gross profit dollars; the plan follows PAR's. Near-term catalysts: Nasdaq relisting (HEC had launched a SPAC with Nasdaq's former CEO and chairman as a director) and index-inclusion forced buying.

notes.title: March 2020 Interim Update
notes.text: First introduced here as USA Technologies (USAT): the largest provider of electronic payments for vending machines and unattended retail, collecting a monthly fee plus a share of revenue; card-enabled machines are far more profitable than cash-only ones. As the largest player it can offer the best service and lowest prices. Vending is recession-resistant but not pandemic-resistant (a closed school means an idle machine). The main story is an activist, a former JP Morgan CFO with an all-star slate of directors to replace a historically mismanaging board, who was expected to take control at the late-April annual meeting.

stocks.summary: Vending and unattended-retail payments software, held in 2020-21 and again from 2024. He saw about $60M of FCF at the FY2026 EBITDA target and a high-teens growth rate; it was taken private in Q2 2025 at a price he found disappointing.

stocks.name: Hill International

notes.title: March 2020 Interim Update
notes.text: Asset-light construction management firm whose shares fell sharply because of Middle East exposure (about 30% of backlog), as investors extrapolated lower oil prices into less Middle East construction. The price is far below his estimate of the value of the U.S. business alone. He attributes the violence of the move to nearly 50% of shares being held by long-term holders, a limited float that makes the stock very sensitive to one panicked seller.

notes.title: YE 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-6; the stock went nowhere in 2019 despite improving metrics (a table in the letter shows gross profit up, adjusted EBITDA swinging from -$1.5M to $21.1M annualized, net debt down, backlog up 11% and 18 insider buys). Management signaled Q4 would be good; clearing the next quarter puts it in the Russell 2000 rebalance, where index buying without regard to price could re-rate it (its removal caused a ~30% drop). Directors have previously called for a sale.

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Presented as a case study. Asset-light construction management on mega projects (an airport, wastewater plants, hospitals), cost-saving for clients, lumpy but less cyclical than assumed. Activists removed the founding family and insiders owned nearly 40% and were still buying. The stock was thrown out of the indexes and off the NYSE after a benign foreign-currency restatement, forcing index and quant selling. The 8th-largest U.S. construction manager; grew revenue through the financial crisis and can buy small rivals cheaply in a downturn. Under-scaled international operations drag margins; cleaned-up cost structure should run at $20-25M of EBITDA versus a near-zero trailing figure; the family had been taking about half of profits, with company cars and golf memberships in the P&L. Even at a 30-40% discount to transaction multiples he saw 60-70% upside, with up to 200% from selling under-scaled pieces and the capital structure. No sell-side coverage and a market cap near $160M, so it is invisible to quants until trailing numbers normalize. So far a meaningful drag: after relisting, a large holder dumped shares (rumored redemptions), and insider buying lowered the free float so the stock was not re-added to indexes.

notes.title: H1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Down with BXC on irrelevant trailing numbers (EV/EBIT 190x on the databases; about 5x EBIT in a few quarters). He compares his position to the 'second-best hand at the table': forced selling after the delisting followed by more forced selling. Fundamentals are improving and insiders are buying 'ravenously'; he doubled down and pitched it at Value X Vail (deck attached). Top-5.

notes.title: Hill International presentation, Value X Vail 2019
notes.text: June 2019 deck (HIL at $2.69 on 6/14/2019; 55.9M shares, market cap ~$150M, cash $27.8M, debt $48.9M, EV ~$172M, insiders ~36%, 52-week range $2.11-6.11). 8th-largest U.S. construction-management-for-fee firm, asset light with no construction risk, >10,000 projects managed (>$500B), founded 1976, public via SPAC in 2006; 2018 revenue by region: Middle East $133.7M, U.S. $205.1M, Europe $41.3M, Africa $26.6M, Latin America $11.5M, Asia/Pacific $10.5M. Long-dated mega projects (SFO $7.3B, Mumbai rail $4B, Pennsylvania DOT $21.7B), low capex, and consolidation (about 300-540 E&C deals a year) that lets scale players buy small rivals in downturns. Negatives: cyclical aspects, low barriers at the bottom, people are the assets. Why mispriced: the founding Richter family ran it like a piggy bank (high pay, country-club memberships, two cars, alleged unauthorized investments and loans, litigation pending), a scattered acquisition strategy left under-scaled regions with negative EBIT (2018 EBIT $42.2M total versus $47.5M excluding negative regions), and four years of drama (2015 go-private bids of $5.50 and $4.75, Bulldog proxy fights, Ancora's call for a sale, a foreign-exchange restatement, NYSE suspension and relisting, the Construction Claims Group sale at about 1x sales, a $40M profit-improvement plan). Selling was non-economic: the delisting forced index and quant selling (over 40% of float, -32%), a vocal holder dumped after relisting (rumored redemptions, -37%), and index gaming failed when HIL was not re-added to the Russell 2000 (-17%). Middle East was ~50% of 2015 revenue; OPEC price up ~70% since 2016 suggests a rebound. A ~$44M Libya receivable (partially paid) is valued at zero. SG&A fell from $170.7M to a ~$120M run rate (28% of revenue); backlog about $0.8B. Insiders bought 1.31M shares (~2.3% of shares outstanding) at $2.22-3.24, at times over half the daily volume. Valuation: U.S. alone at 1.0x sales gives $3.29 (+22%) and at 8x EBITDA $3.71 (+38%); 2021 baseline (5% growth, 9% EBITDA margin, 8x) $4.51 (+67%); the 2015 bid multiple of 0.65x on 2018 sales gives $4.64 (+72%); sale at 0.65-1.05x sales $4.60-7.67 (+71% to +185%); simplified sale including a buyback up to $8.20 (+205%). Peers trade near 11.5x EBITDA versus about 5-6x for HIL. A sale seems likely but not necessary: Engine, Crescendo, Ancora and the Richters have all called for one. Risks: cyclical slowdown, oil, execution.

notes.title: YE 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Upsized because of the imminent relisting, which he now calls a mistake; the stock fell about 30% after relisting. A large holder (reported to face redemptions) and tax-loss sellers weighed in late in the year. Insiders (directors and management) bought heavily; $40M cost savings; 10+ potential buyers; a tea-leaves timeline around Jacobs Engineering (ex-CEO Craig Martin left Hill's board on Oct 18, 2018, three days before Jacobs said it would sell its energy business and focus on infrastructure, with M&A as a use of proceeds). He added to the position.

notes.title: Q3 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New large position (HILI/HIL): asset-light construction manager and consultant (47% of 2017 revenue U.S., 35% Middle East) that operates cost-plus. Delisted from the NYSE in August after a 3-year currency-translation restatement, dropping about 30% overnight as index and quant holders were forced out; it became current on October 12 and expected to relist and hold its first investor call in over a year on October 18. Activist Ancora (about 2 years) bought more and nominated a director; founding family removed; a profit plan targeting about $40M of savings against a roughly $260M EV; target EBITDA margins of 10-12%. Comps at about 1x sales and 10.5x EBITDA; 1x U.S. sales almost justifies the EV, so the international business is nearly free; about $6 a share on 1x guided sales; holders of almost 50% want a sale; NV5 trades at over 20x EBITDA, so a successful consolidator could reach the high teens. He knew he was operating with incomplete information (possible 'more than one cockroach').

stocks.summary: Asset-light construction management firm bought after an NYSE de-listing; relist and international assets were the angle.

stocks.name: Gaia

notes.title: YE 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Hit $22+ then fell over 50% into year-end as analysts reacted to rising customer acquisition cost. He says the increase is transitory or revenue-generating: a new event space, language translation, and a push into Alternative Healing. The subscription price rose 20%. The company could be profitable on 30 days' notice by slowing growth spending; yoga participation rose through the financial crisis. Success means 500-700% upside; downside is capped by real estate and IP.

notes.title: Q1 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Completed an equity offering that diluted the fund, which he likes: demand from larger investors who were waiting for a raise, 4x oversubscription, more liquidity, insider purchases, research coverage (one bank at a $23 target), falling customer acquisition costs (25-30% of growth is word of mouth), a possible subscription price increase and monetizing the 'Truth Seeker' community (it petitioned for an event space on its campus). He thinks upside could exceed the $60 a share he projected for 2021.

notes.title: YE 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Up about 100% since purchase, so he trimmed the position (still large). The company is executing against a plan for $2.50 EPS in 2021 and the model is proving sustainable.

notes.title: H1 2017 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Growing faster than expected while spending less on growth. International subscribers (foreign-language expansion) became a larger share of the total than domestic. A first 'Truth Seekers' customer gathering was a big success; he sees Comic-Con-style monetization of the community. Heading toward 1.6M subscribers and $2.50 EPS (several hundred percent upside); if it slowed growth it would be profitable now.

notes.title: Seeking Alpha PRO interview (April 2017)
notes.text: His example of cash that is worth more than its face value: the CEO is the largest shareholder, frugal, with a strong capital-allocation record and a plan to spend cash on customer acquisition only up to 50% of customer lifetime value, which is the equivalent of requiring a 100% return. Contrasted with net-nets where cash is drained by high salaries. A hard catalyst: the next 10-Q would completely change the balance sheet.

notes.title: YE 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New and a top-5 holding: a streaming service for yoga, 'seeking truth' and transformation (7,200 hours of content, 93% exclusive; $9.95 a month; about 170,000 subscribers; content costs under 20% of revenue vs about 70% at Netflix). It grew revenue over 50% a year and loses money only because acquisition costs are expensed up front. Bought after the company sold its yoga-products business for $167M and its travel unit for $12.85M, then ran a tender offer ($7.75 a share; undersubscribed, so about $75M bought about 40% of the company). Stale 10-Q numbers hid about $77M of cash (about 81% of the market cap) and a Louisville, Colorado campus (carried at $17.2M, he estimates $28-34M), so the video business cost less than zero at $6.25. CEO and 38% owner Jirka Rysavy (Corporate Express founder) did not tender. Targets: 1M subscribers in 2019 and 1.6M in 2021, giving $60M pre-tax and $2.50 EPS (his 20-25x P/E implies $50-62.50); steady-state value $8-11.50; liquidation value $6.24-$8.76. notes.title: Q3 2017 Letter to Partners

notes.title: H1 2017 Letter to Partners

notes.title: Seeking Alpha PRO interview (April 2017)
notes.text: Used as his example of large insider ownership: Ron Perelman owned about 78% and Revlon traded at a severe multiple discount to peers. Bears say it will never get a comp multiple because of Perelman; he says it does not need one given operational improvements including integrating Elizabeth Arden. notes.title: YE 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Flat on the year after a wild ride. He presented a deck at the Manual of Ideas/Lattice Work Best Ideas Conference and said his confidence had grown.

notes.title: Q2 2016 Letter to Partners
notes.text: $1.7B market cap but Perelman owns 78%, leaving only about $350M of float (under 50,000 shares trade a day), so the stock trades at about half its peers' EV/EBITDA (8x forward on core Revlon at about $32). Argument: a sale is not needed. Perelman hired Fabian Garcia from Colgate (9th CEO, $1.5M salary, 150% bonus, $10M stock grant), plans shareholder engagement for the first time, added $100M to advertising, and the Elizabeth Arden deal doubles sales from 2013 to 2016 (19% CAGR) with 2019 adjusted EBITDA above $700M. Elizabeth Arden: $250M of cosmetics/skin sales at Revlon's 20% margin justifies 75% of the price; fragrances (over $700M of sales) cost about $220M, 0.3x sales vs Inter Parfums at 1.8x; $140M cost synergies (management expects $100M in year 1). Leverage 4.2x with synergies (5.7x without); platform comps (Middleby, Fleetcor, Zayo, CIMPRESS, TransDigm) average 16.6x versus Revlon at 7.3x. Exit scenarios: at 12x in 12 years $132 / $258 / $440 a share; a sale in 7 years $180 / $267 / $364. Shares had fallen 12% in the quarter when the strategic review became an acquisition rather than a sale.

stocks.summary: Cosmetics company controlled by Perelman, held 2016-17 on an EV/EBITDA and platform-growth thesis.

notes.title: Q1 2021 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Mid-sized new position re-bought in early 2021 after an earlier loss-making sale: about 90% share in third-party Oracle/SAP support; expects a re-rating once the Oracle litigation clears.

notes.title: Q3 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Shares rallied about 50% from his price, then fell below it when a Nevada court granted Oracle a permanent injunction (mid-August), stayed about a month later pending the 9th Circuit appeal, and rallied again. He calls it noise: the court already ruled that third-party support providers may exist, and the 9th Circuit earlier vacated an injunction (Judge Friedland, a former Munger, Tolles partner, questioned the need for it). Complying would cost only 1-4% of gross margin (a 46-49% savings pitch instead of 50%); Oracle subpoenaed about 1,200 of 1,500 customers yet revenue retention stayed above 90%. He thinks Rimini should keep prices low and build relationships now, as scale could let it become a long-term compounder; he added on weakness. The RMNIW warrants swung wildly (200 warrants traded at $1.00 vs $0.62, creating about $5.6M of 'market value' from $200).

notes.title: H1 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New: the idea he prepared for Value X Vail (deck attached). Third-party support for enterprise software, defensive and counter-cyclical with high normalized margins and fast growth, but exposed to Oracle's litigation. He bought at very low prices after employees sold en masse once the post-earnings trading window opened (May 10), right after the Russell rebalance record date (May 11), knowing index funds would buy six weeks later at a price set when shares were 30%+ higher. He owns common stock and the SPAC warrants (RMNIW), up over 30% in about a month; he says the warrants, essentially long-dated options, would be the right bet even at a 95% chance of zero, and could return 10-30x.

notes.title: Rimini Street presentation, Value X Vail 2018
notes.text: 2018 Value X Vail deck (RMNI and its SPAC warrants RMNIW). Leading third-party maintenance provider for enterprise software (Oracle, SAP), at about half the vendor's price; 1,500+ customers including 70 Fortune 500 and 20 Fortune Global 100; ~$3B saved; customer satisfaction 4.8/5; 100% subscription revenue with 93% retention; counter-cyclical (Oracle grew support revenue through the Great Recession). Public via the GP Investments SPAC in October 2017. Snapshot: ~62M shares, ~$373M market cap, ~$37M cash, ~$140M convertible preferred, EV ~$476M, 73% insider-owned, only ~10% free float and ~30k shares a day. Revenue $118M (2015), $160M (2016), $213M (2017); gross margin 55% to 61%. Why mispriced: GAAP expenses customer acquisition up front (LTV/CAC above 5x but softening from 7.7x to 5.8x), one sell-side analyst, no roadshow, and employees who could sell for the first time after Q1 dumped shares. Growth stumbled (2017 revenue $212M versus $220M guided; 2018 guide cut to ~$260M versus $295M) because the legacy 15% lender covenants limited spending; a June 19 convertible preferred offering retired that debt, saving ~$95M over three years. Litigation: Oracle won ~$75-100M in 'Rimini I' (about $65-90M adjusted for interest); 'Rimini II' lets Rimini counter-sue for unfair competition; a federal subpoena also arrived. The court held that the right to provide 3PM is not in question, only the process, and 70+ Fortune 500 legal teams and several PE funds reviewed it. He assumes a $100M liability. Litigation also deters under-capitalized entrants. Insiders: CEO Seth Ravin owns ~21-23% (earlier ran TomorrowNow, which Oracle litigated to death), CIO Thomas Shay ~9%, Adams Street ~39%, GP Investments. Valuation at $6: EV ~$613M including litigation reserve, 2.4x 2018 sales and 1.8x 2019E; steady-state EBIT $92M pre-litigation (6.7x) and $67M after (9.2x); $10 equals 2.7x 2019E revenue (+66%). 2022 scenarios: growth disappoints $8-12 (+36% to +106%), continued growth $13-24 (+117% to +300%), focus on cash flow $28-36; disaster scenario -100% for stock, which is why the warrants (upside effectively capped at an $18 stock price) are an attractive skew. Risks: worse legal result, new competition after resolution, dilution (including $11.50 warrants), PE sponsors needing liquidity.

stocks.name: Flotek

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Case study of a mistake in sizing. Oilfield services: a patent-protected chemistry business that raises drillers' ROI plus a commoditized fluids business; not great but not terrible, and bought at almost nothing. Essentially a cash shell, so management matters: new Chairman David Nierenberg (ex-Bain, ran Pacific Northwest fund raising for Romney, small-cap activist fund manager for decades, board roles at the Washington state pension, Glass Lewis and Columbia governance) was seen as unlikely to plunder cash. The company had about $80M market cap and $45M net debt, then sold one division for $170M (about 23x EBITDA), so it actually held about $120M net cash, which screeners had not yet picked up; the stock doubled in January. He sold some near $3.50-3.60 while Nierenberg bought, then bought more expecting a capital return; the company then declined a tender offer, saying a dollar in their hands is worth more given capital-starved oil and gas, and the stock fell over 30%, needing an 80% rise to return to Nierenberg's purchase level. He says he was too cute and sized it too large. Old sales force was paid on revenue and sometimes shipped at a loss; sales is moving to chemical engineers. Escape hatch: three of eight listed peers were acquired at about 1x sales versus about 0.1x for FTK. Oil spike is a free option (it was a $30 stock five years earlier, $2 now).

notes.title: H1 2019 Letter to Partners
notes.text: Top-5. Bought below net current asset value with two-thirds of market cap in cash after selling one of two segments for about 150% more than the whole company's EV. Sized large from the outset; shares rose about 25% then faded, leaving a slight gain. He treats it as near-cash with a free option on a frac-drilling business better than its industry, run by an incentivized allocator who bought more shares. Cash was not returned after Q1 earnings because the strategic review was unfinished; he expects a return with Q2 earnings and will then re-underwrite.

notes.title: Q1 2019 Letter to Partners

New chairman is a known allocator, a new CFO with a record of short stints at companies in change, and the CEO took a 70% pay cut (but has a ~$7M golden parachute). A strategic review with an investment bank; peers sold at 1.2x sales versus 0.3x pro forma, so over 200% upside to a buyer. He expects quant models to buy it once the Q1 10-Q shows the cash, which he likens to 'the Terminator' (model after the GAIA setup).

notes.title: Greenhill presentation, MOI Best Ideas 2018
notes.text: 2018 Best Ideas deck, a 'stub stock' special situation (GHL at $18.50, 27.4M shares, market cap ~$506M, cash $278M, debt $350M, EV ~$578M, insiders ~17%, yield 1.1%, 52-week range $13.80-32.45; the slide footnote dates the price 12/28 and reads 2016, apparently a typo for 2017). Boutique M&A advisory firm (founded 1996, IPO 2004) with restructuring, capital raising and the Cogent PE-secondary business added in 2015; 78 client-facing MDs. Likes: conflict-free advice, virtually zero capex, boutiques taking share, cash flow through the cycle (about $93M a year of net income plus stock comp on average, around $86M adjusted for the current structure and ex-merchant bank), and a history of buying back shares to offset dilution while peers' share counts balloon. Dislikes: low barriers, 'body shop' (assets ride the elevator), slower growth than peers, 2017 nine-month revenue down about 26% to ~$172M, lumpier and more large-deal and non-U.S. weighted than peers. It was a contest-winning short idea on VIC in May 2014 at $50 and 32x P/E (peak ~$95); now ~6x a 10-year average adjusted cash flow with the dividend cut about 90%. Special situation: in September 2017 it announced a levered recap, a $350M 5-year term loan at L+375, a buyback of up to $285M including a 12M-share tender at $17.25, a 90% dividend cut, $10M of new equity each from the CEO and chairman and a 90% CEO salary cut for $2.75M of stock. The tender was undersubscribed (3.4M shares, ~12%, for $59.2M), so no true stub, but about $226M (~45% of market cap) of dry powder is earmarked for buybacks and no one sold at $17.25 or below. Insiders gave up roughly $40M of dividends and salary; the CEO had said in 2011 that cutting the dividend would take waterboarding. The 10-Q cited backlog signaling significant improvement into 2018 (the last such reference was Q3 2015, before 2016 revenue rose 28% and shares ~90%); nine MDs hired in 2017 and inbound interest from competitors' senior bankers; Barclays' global head of restructuring hired. M&A cycle: PE dry powder and a possible slowdown help boutiques; seesaw set-up where a lower price now means more shares retired. Valuation: if 2018 equals 2016 (revenue $335.5M, EBIT margin 27.2%), EPS is about $1.97 before buybacks and up to $3.28 with 40% fewer shares; 13-18x implies $26-59 (+38% to +219%). Average cash flow 2014-16 at 8-12x gives $23-34; 2007-16 at 8-12x $25-38. A 2022 normal year (103 MDs at $4M each) gives EPS $2.85-4.75 and $37-100 a share at 13-21x; a dividend-resumption exercise gives $45-122. Risks: failing to buy back stock, losing top performers, weak recruit productivity, index funds selling as float shrinks, the first reduced dividend on 12/20/17, tax-bill uncertainty.

notes.title: YE 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: A big winner that reversed in the last two months of the year (down about 66% in Q4). Higher mortgage rates mean fewer originations, but Ocwen had been barred from buying MSRs and will be able to again after moving to a new servicing platform in 2-3 quarters. Leon Cooperman closing Omega Advisors and a filing showing Omega's international fund selling triggered a drop; most of his stake would survive in other entities. notes.title: Q1 2018 Letter to Partners
notes.text: New large position: hated mortgage servicer after a ~90% fall, a decade of mismanagement and regulatory fines. More than 70 mortgage-bond investors wrote ratings agencies supporting its servicing; it has modified more mortgages than any other servicer. Bought near $3 against his estimate of $5-9 economic book value, with selling pressure from the founder's option trade (10M shares of calls at $2.50-$3.00, hedged by a bank). Catalysts: regulators lifting the ban on buying MSRs, rising rates lengthening MSR cash flows, the PHH acquisition (moving to Black Knight), industry consolidation (WMIH with $6B of NOLs merging with Nationstar; Ditech next, with Cooperman owning over 10% of OCN and almost 50% of DHCP), and a possible move to sub-servicing. A combined OCN-PHH-DHCP might trade at $8-12. Credit to David Rosenblum of Prophet Capital. He adds that a return to post-WWII housing trends is not needed for success.

stocks.name: Interview themes (Seeking Alpha PRO, April 2017)

notes.title: Seeking Alpha PRO interview (April 2017)
notes.text: Looks for 'good co/bad co' set-ups, where GAAP nets a profitable segment with a loss-making one (a segment earning $1.00 plus one losing $0.75 shows $0.25; closing the loser quadruples reported earnings), and SaaS companies whose acquisition costs are expensed up front. Wants management aligned through equity ownership, proxy pay and capital allocation, 'as if the money is their own'. Large insider stakes are often penalized by the market for low float, which he treats as time arbitrage. Base-case valuation should include no multiple expansion. Not a cigar-butt approach: margin of safety should grow over time. Catalysts are nice but not required; patience is key. Prefers holdings that can benefit when things go wrong (defensive cash flows, strong balance sheet, good capital allocators). Market timing is a losing game; smaller investors should keep picking up rocks.

notes.text: Three ideas guide him: with the economy shut down, balance sheets outrank income statements (he had not considered revenue going to zero at any holding; some babies are being thrown out with the bathwater, but he cannot pick bottoms, and a stock bought at 3x midcycle earnings can go to 2x); like Forrest Gump after the storm, own businesses that gain share in a downturn; and aim for 'enough' returns instead of waiting for the last nickel, noting credit card stocks rose 300-400% before delinquencies peaked after March 2009. No portfolio leverage and long-term partner commitments let him decide when to buy. Most of his family's wealth stays in the strategy and he planned to add.

notes.title: 2019 Limited Partner Meeting transcript
notes.text: Said the best advantage of a partnership is a high-quality LP base (professional investors, entrepreneurs, former executives, skilled professionals) who understand volatility is not risk; about 24% of AUM from friends and family; he and his wife are essentially all-in; almost all partners have multi-year commitments. Staying small helps (a table of the young Buffett). Top 10 positions are usually 75-85% of capital; none in the S&P 500 and only a handful in the Russell 2000. Headwinds: small caps, low volatility, growth over value, and hedge-fund small-cap-value exposure near all-time lows (he quotes Cliff Asness on value). Process: a good business that will look similar in ten years, aligned management, resilience when things go wrong, and understanding why the opportunity exists, plus margin of safety, patience (Greenblatt, Buffett) and decision quality (Annie Duke). He passed on The Joint Corp (franchised chiropractic) at about 90x earnings as not a true subscription business with no barriers to entry; it rose 250-300% afterward, which he calls a mistake of omission, not of process. Plan: keep doing the same, as stocks can go nowhere for 2-3 years and then jump.

profile: Laughing Water Capital is a small, concentrated long-only equity fund (Laughing Water Capital, LP and, since 2021, Laughing Water Capital II, LP) run by Matt Sweeney, CFA, Managing Partner of LW Capital Management, LLC, from a base about 40 minutes outside New York City. The fund began on February 8, 2016. It writes to partners about twice a year and its auditor is Spicer Jeffries.

How it invests: about 15 stocks, mostly small and micro caps, in good businesses facing temporary operating, optical or structural problems and led by incentivized management, often with insider buying. He says he buys at 'special-situation prices', thinks 3-5 years ahead and gives little weight to macro forecasts. Recurring themes in the letters are spectrum assets, asset-light homebuilding, restaurant software, CDMOs and SaaS.
He says he and his family have nearly all their wealth invested alongside partners and that he has turned away more capital than he accepted to keep the fund small.
